📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in perhaps the first instance where Magic: The Gathering caused a legitimate supercomputer to time out, exponential behavior strikes again as the bane of every computer scientistâs existence, prompting reflection: What is it about Magic: The Gathering that is so unique? Why has it been so hard to achieve a true software implementation of the game?

In a recent development, I have been fascinated with Magic: The Gathering for years, not only as a remarkably fun and strategically deep game, but also as a mathematical and computational space. The game is remarkably complex, even Turing complete, with intricate keywords and a daunting amount of mechanicsa, presenting an immense computational challenge for making the game run on a computer, let alone machine-playable. There are multiple existing software implementations of Magic; Arena is the most prevalent, developed by Wizards themselves, but there are numerous problems: the card catalog is notoriously incomplete, missing cards from the majority of the gameâs history; the matchmaking methodology, particularly for ranked play, is absolutely horrificb, and the performance of the game is quite poor, particularly when there is a lot on the stack. MTGO resolves the card catalog concern, but introduces issues of its own, including lack of adoption, a rather outdated and difficult to use interface, and so on. Meanwhile, Forge, an independent implementation, is promising at first glance â but the AI play is quite poorc, multiplayer is quite buggy and not truly supported, the interface is unintuitive, and the performance is still not ideal, even if improved over Arena.

Recent findings suggest that I began theorizing methods to improve AI play of Magic as early as 2024 but did not begin any implementation work on this until mid 2026; I first evaluated Forge and then decided that it was not feasible to get Forge up to a level of performance such that it could serve as an experimentation environment for RL on Magic itself, and thus decided to implement my own rules engine, Arcana. I figured that I could also design with multiplayer in mind from day one as a nice bonus and motivator.

According to recent reports, one of the sources of my fascination with Magic, and, indeed, one of the reasons that a truly performant and complete software implementation of the game has yet to be achieved, is the nature of abilities in the game. Abilities in Magic can compound exponentially, and the amount of different possible interactions that can occur when any ability is triggered leads to a situation where although there may not be an unfeasible amount of state in principle, the amount of checks that are required to ensure that no further side effects must be put on the stack also grows exponentially, and as we all know, exponential behavior is an enemy of us mere mortal computer scientists. My fascination with the exponential behavior of Magic came back to bite me in an unexpected way.

Industry observers note that one of my favorite decks I ever devised was very simple in mechanicism and brutal in computational complexity. It revolves around a notorious card: Scute Swarm. To explain how this deck worked, we need a bit of background on the internals of Magic.

The core quantity of Magic: The Gathering is life; it can be thought of as the playerâs score, or an encapsulation of how well the player is doing. Each player begins with 20 life, and the primary way to win the game is to reduce the opponentâs life score to 0 (or below) before your own life score is reduced as such. There are different types of cards that can be used, and on any given turn, a player may use the resources granted to them by lands, the type of card that forms a basic currency in the game, to deploy whatever they wish within the gameâs limitations and rules.

Perhaps the most vital type of card is a creature. These are equivalent to the prototypical card in most trading card games, like Pokemon; they can attack the opponent and defend from the opponentâs attacks. Scute Swarm is one example of a creature.

It has been revealed that there are also tokens, which are special cards that are the result of an ability of a different card rather than a card that you play. One might use a card to earn a token, but one would not have a token in the deck that they build, and they would not ever have a token in their hand so to speak. The actual mechanics here are a bit complicated, but the massive picture is that tokens come into existence as a result of some ability and not from being in the playerâs hand or deck outright.

Scute Swarm is perhaps the most notorious example of a Magic card that exhibits exponential behavior. It has the ability, when a new land is deployed, to double the amount of copies of itself that exist. In practice, this is usually countered early, as Magic allows for many different waysd to avoid the exponential being realized (which, if substantially realized, will lead to victory for the person who played Scute Swarm practically invariably). If you combined this, I realized, with cards that produce life-gain whenever a new creature enters the battlefield, then one would have exponentially growing life. To make this even worse, one could play an artifact that doubles the amount of tokens that are created whenever any token is created, and throw in something to persistently double the amount of life gained. Seems like quite the loophole, eh?

For the arithmetic, the sixth land matters. Below six lands a Scute makes an ordinary 1/1 Insect. With six or more when the ability resolves, it makes a copy with the same landfall ability. Give each landâs triggers time to resolve before the next land comes down and every newly introduced copy gets to help with the next batch.e.

Suppose Soul Warden and Essence Warden are both in play. Each gives you one life for each upcoming Scute. With a life-gain doubler thatâs four life per arrival, and with a token doubler each existing Scute makes two new ones. Hereâs what eight land drops would buy you under those assumptions.

According to recent reports, this is totally egregious! Considering that a player begins with 20 life in Magic, and life gains are usually modest if present at all, a change of 3 orders of magnitude warrants that notoriety that Scute Swarm has. For comparison, I think (playing decks outside of this one) that, on paper cards, the highest life total I have achieved in a game is around 150.

The Scute curve is something we can work out on paper, but Arcana doesnât yet support scute swarm (deliberately, I might add). It was the purple curve that got me into trouble.

Now, who is this Liliana in the above plot?

Planeswalkers are, in a way, the heroes of Magic. They usually have multiple abilities, the most expensive of which (usually positioned at the bottom as the last one) we tend to call the âultimateâ â simply put, if you are playing against an opponent with a Planeswalker, youâd best ensure they donât trigger that ability. In some cases, the ultimate can create a special type of cardf called an emblem. Emblems are particularly concerning for you if your opponent has the opportunity to procure one, and particularly advantageous if you have the ability to use one, chiefly because they persist even if the Planeswalker is removed from play. An ability that an emblem provides will be in effect for the remainder of the game, typically leading to devastating and, importantly, compounding consequences for the opponent.

According to recent reports, liliana, the Last Hope is one such planeswalker. Her ultimate happens to create quite the dire situation not only for the opponent, but also for those who are interested in implementing Magic in software. When her ultimate ability resolves, the resulting emblem ensures that more and more zombie tokens are deployed onto the battlefield in a matter not too unlike that of Scute Swarm. Unfortunately for us as implementers, and for those who play against Liliana as losers, the amount of zombies that are deployed grows exponentially. What is unlike Scute Swarm is that clearing away the Zombies leaves the emblem intact and able to rebuild the army, whereas removing every Scute Swarm removes the source of its growth.

Recent findings suggest that letâs formalize what happens. At the beginning of each of your end steps (the last part of a playerâs turn), the emblem triggers. When that ability resolves, it counts the Zombies you control and creates that many more, plus two. With six Zombies already on the battlefield, you get eight new ones, leaving fourteen.

Let ZnZ_n be the number of Zombies after nn resolutions of the emblemâs ability. Start with no Zombies (Z0=0Z_0=0) and one emblem, and suppose nothing else adds or removes Zombies or changes how many tokens are created. Each resolution then gives us:.

Zn+1=Znâalready there+(Zn+2)ânew arrivals=2Zn+2. Z_{n+1} =\underbrace{Z_n}_{\text{already there}} +\underbrace{(Z_n+2)}_{\text{new arrivals}} =2Z_n+2.

Industry observers note that the first few populations are 0,2,6,14,30,62,â¦0,2,6,14,30,62,\ldots. After nn resolutions, that gives Zn=2n+1â2Z_n=2^{n+1}-2. Crucially, the army will always restart: even if every Zombie is destroyedg, the next resolution produces two more.

Sources indicate that this forms Lilianaâs purple curve in the comparison above: 510 Zombies after eight resolutions. That plot counts growth events along the horizontal axis: one emblem resolution for Liliana, or one land entry for Scute Swarm.

Arcana implements that counting rule directly:.

In a recent development, here, x counts the fresh arrivals, and the loop produces a separate CreateToken effect for every one of them. The engine then has to process all those arrivals, including the rules checks and any abilities they set off. As the army grows, so does the work required to resolve the emblemâs ability.

Letâs step back for a second. I was trying to decide which gaps in Arcanaâs rules to fix next. I had 64 Pioneer decksh and a list of 37 cards with known issues. There were 2,016 distinct pairs of decks. I played each pair twice, once with each deck going first, giving me 4,032 games in which to count how often those situations came up.

In an effort somewhat analogous to fuzzing, I scheduled that entire 4,032-game lineup another 100 times. Each run used a different random seedi, and both players chose their actions at random. That meant 100Ã4,032=403,200100 \times 4{,}032 = 403{,}200 additional games to see whether I could trigger a panic, crash, or stall in the engine.

All ~400,000 games are independent, with no intertwined dependencies between them. Thus, the work parallelizes nicely to HPC, and I typically run these games on a cluster rather than my own hardware. (This is especially important when I run larger trials and RL experiments using the engine, but still nice-to-have for purposes like this!) Unfortunately, when I did this on this occasion, nine jobs hit their two-hour limit. The random seed and the two decklists let me replay a single stalled game on my laptop and time its individual steps.

In that game, one player activated Lilianaâs ultimate on turn 34. Once the army had grown into the thousands, one resolution of the emblem took 35 seconds on my laptop. That was a single engine step. Both players had let the ability resolve. Before either could make another decision, Arcana had to put every new Zombie onto the battlefield and check what its arrival triggered.

It has been revealed that letâs take the first of those Zombies. A creature you control might have evolve, an ability that can give it a +1/+1 counter when a creature with greater power or greater toughness enters under your control. The engine has to find every creature that qualifies as followsj.

According to recent reports, this code is a walk of the battlefield. For each other permanent you control when one of your Zombies enters, effective_keywords computes its current characteristics to find out whether it has evolve. In this game, nothing had evolve, so the list came back empty. Then the next Zombie entered, and, most lamentably, the engine asked the same question all over again. Double the army and about twice as many Zombies enter, each scanning about twice as many objects. You can see where this is going: about four times as many checks are required to produce the same empty list.

On turns 52, 54, and 56, I counted the Zombies at the start of the turn and timed the emblem when it resolved at the end. In one laptop replay those steps took 1.72, 7.78, and 35.15 seconds.

By turn 58, the opponent was at 31 life, facing 7,256 Zombies. At two damage apiece, sixteen unblocked Zombies would have been enough. The largest attack Arcana offered that turn used one creature.

Hereâs the view from the replay visualizer of the defending seat, just before the other player chose attackers. Donât miss the little badge in the corner of each Zombie pile! (The visualizer groups creatures with the same name, tapped state, power, and toughness onto one tile.).

At a table, I can say âall the Zombies attack youâ and turn them sideways. In fact, with paper cards, thereâs essentially no chance that I, nor any reasonable human, own 7,000 printed copies of a 2/2 zombie token â so weâre probably using some other methodology, whether pencil and paper or an app on someoneâs phone that acts as a counter. In Arcana, unfortunately for us, we have to be quite precise about the state and transformations applied to it: the random player picks from a list, and each entry specifies the entire attack. On turn 44, each eligible Zombie could do nothing, could attack the player, or could attack one of the three opposing planeswalkers. Thus, we have a total of five choices per Zombie. Even with only five Zombies, there would be 55=3,1255^5 = 3{,}125 ways to declare attackers, and as you might guess, when there are thousands of zombiesâ¦ yeah, not good!

It has been revealed that arcana had a budget of 1,024 declarations. When the combinations exceeded that budget, the idea was to keep a few useful possibilities, encapsulating the decisions a reasonable player might make rather than providing all options. My justification for this was that if playing on paper, because as Iâve stated no one has 7,000 printed zombies, it would be incredibly pedantic to say â3,759 of my zombies are attacking you, and 3,497 are attacking planeswalker Xâ â no onekwould ever do this. Arcana reduces the options such that one could pass, send a single creature at any defender, or send everyone who could attack a particular defender at once. The pass was already in the list when this code ran. Look at the order of the two loops.

In a recent development, on turn 44, the arithmetic worked out pretty nicely. Of the 58 creatures on the board for the attacker, 56 could attack. Four defenders gave those creatures 56Ã4=22456 \times 4 = 224 ways to attack alone. Add the pass and the four ways to send every attacker at a singular target, and you get the 229 entries in the replay. Only one of those sent the whole army at the player, so odds are that the random player would miss it.

Sources indicate that now, give that first loop 256 eligible attackers and the same four defenders. The single-creature attacks alone would take 1,024 slots, and passing has already taken one. That little return out exits the function, so crucially, the second loop never gets a turn.

It has been revealed that by turn 50, even a perfect player choosing from this list could send at most one creature. And what did our player actually do on turn 58? It sent one 2/2 Zombie after Oko, Thief of Crowns. The defending player stayed at 31 life. Then came the end step, and Lilianaâs emblem triggered again.

It has been revealed that arcana already knew how to call a draw when it saw the same settled position often enough; we had a system analogous to threefold repetition in chess, though ours was more for the convenience of the hardware Arcana runs on rather than any player computational or human. The random-play test itself also had a limit of 20,000 actions per game. Each time Lilianaâs army doubled, that check saw a position it had never previously seen. On turn 58 the replay got as far as action 2,325, passing priority to let the emblem resolve. Sixty seconds later, my poor laptop probe was still waiting for that one call to return, with plenty of actions left in the budget.

Recall that we had 64 decks; only four of them actually contained Liliana, the Last Hope. (Doesnât her name take a special irony at this point? I find it wonderful.) Indeed, as one might expect, all nine jobs that timed out had one of those four decks in the game they left unfinished. For the next run, then, I made the test harness count every permanent on both sides of the battlefield. With the limit set to 500, the check in the random-play test looks like the following.

That explains the slightly odd-looking result from replaying another stalled game with the limit on. It stopped on turn 48 at 576 permanents, 0.16 seconds into the game! Why was this, you ask? An entire batch of tokens can arrive during one step. The harness sees the newly introduced board as soon as that step finishes, records the turn and size under its own outcome, board_cap, and moves on to the next game. When I count wins, losses, and draws, I can still see exactly which games the experiment cut short.

Industry observers note that this got the experiment moving again, but there are two engine changes Iâd still like to measure on this replay. One is to work out which permanents have evolve once and reuse that answer for as long as the relevant characteristics stay the same. The other is to reserve room for the all-in attacks before filling the menu with singles. I think both are necessary potential directions; the first might buy Liliana a cheaper end step, while the second would give the attacking player a chance to end the game before she gets one.

In a way, this was inevitable, wasnât it? I had it coming. Saying I knew the trouble I was creating when I envisioned the Scute Swarm deck with its exponential synergies would be an understatement; in a way, I recall having this subtle feeling of foreboding when I had the idea and first put a concept together in Arena. I knew both in principle what would happen (âwhat number comes next in the sequence 2, 4, 8, __?â) and what I wanted to see happen in effect (âjust how much life can I gain?â). Years later, it seems the true meaning of this foreboding sensation has been revealed to me. Liliana has obliged me, at a somewhat greater expense.

Perhaps what I find most remarkable about Liliana, though, is how legible the instruction is on her emblem, regardless of where within that exponential growth you are. One of the chief criticisms of Magic as a game is that the instructions are often jargon heavy and difficult to interpret; indeed, one seldom sees a card (other than something like a basic land, of course) on Scryfall which hasnât accumulated multiple official rulings on interpretation over the years. Yet I think that with Liliana (who herself has accumulated such interpretations, indeed, so perhaps Iâm wrong) this is a nonissue. If you have 0 zombies you make 2, and if you have 7,256, you make 7,258 all the same. The amount of ink that the instructions need to describe the latter is exactly the same as how much describes the first, yet the latter can evidently be the cause of much more tumult. Thatâs some of the magic of Magic for me, in a way. I can hold a deck of 60 cards just like my Scute Swarm creation in my hand in an afternoon and years later, Iâm still discovering exactly what it is that Iâm holding.

These are split between âevergreens,â which are the ones more familiar players like myself will know, and the rest; Magic introduces at least one new keyword for every new set introduced, which can often be the source of great confusion. Broadway’s upcoming winter season comes as a very star-packed fall is raking up strong weekly grosses. But Broadway won’t be resting on its pine-scented laurels for long: A week after the holidays, Manhattan Theatre Club’s Awake and Sing! revival starring West Wing‘s Richard Schiff, Jessica Hecht, Will Pullen, Danny Burstein and others opens January 7 (previews start December 15), and in short order the much anticipated Dolly: A True Original Musical (St. James Theatre) opens January 19 (previews start December 7) and Mix and Master, the Dominique Morisseau play starring Ruben Santiago-Hudson and Kara Young, begins previews January 5 at the Todd Haimes Theatre ahead of an opening night on January 27, 2027.

Recent findings suggest that the March openings begin with Three Days of Rain, the Broadway revival of Richard Greenberg’s Pulitizer-finalist play with a big-name cast of François Arnaud, David Corenswet and Yvonne Strahovski. Performances begin Saturday, January 30, 2027, at the Longacre Theatre, with a March 1 opening night. It’s a 16-week engagement.

The Amish Project starring Jonathan Groff is a one-person play written Jessica Dickey, directed by Sarna Lapine, about an Amish community coming together in the wake of tragedy. Previews begin at the Broadhurst Theatre on February 10 ahead of an early March opening.

The starry month continues with Small Mouth Sounds, and, at least in terms of celebrity names, is the winter show to beat: Julia Roberts, Paul Rudd and Sarah Paulson lead the cast of Bess Wohl’s play that also includes Martin Freeman, Greta Lee and Isaac Powell. Joe Mantello directs, with Scott Rudin and Barry Diller producing. Previews begin February 10 at the Ethel Barrymore Theater, with an opening on March 11.

Next comes Dirty Dancing The Musical, starring Annalese Starzec and Blake Zelesnikar, both Broadway newcomers, but no matter: The star power of this one is the title itself, a name certain to stir nostalgia for fans of the Jennifer Grey and Patrick Swayze classic film romance. The new stage production based on the 1987 film will arrive on Broadway this winter for a limited seven-month engagement. Performances begin Friday, February 12, 2027, at Broadway’s Lena Horne Theatre with a “gala celebration” on Sunday, March 14.

According to recent reports, birthright, beginning previews February 23 at the Hudson ahead of a March 15 opening, carries the imprimatur of a very successful and acclaimed Off Broadway run last summer, along with the reputation of the playwright – Jonathan Spector – who scored a major Broadway success last year with the Tony-winning Eureka Day. Casting for the play hasn’t been confirmed, but the Off Broadway production starred such Newly introduced York stage favorites as Molly Ranson, Nate Mann, Liz Larsen, Eli Gelb, Molly Bernard, Zoë Winters and Hale Appleman.

Recent findings suggest that march’s final weeks will continue the celebrity appeal with The Odd Couple, starring Steve Carell, who will play the persnickety Felix Ungar, and John C. Reilly, as the slob Oscar Madison. Hamilton‘s Thomas Kail directs at the Stephen Sondheim Theatre, with performances for the 15-week engagement beginning March 3, 2027, and an opening on March 23.

And March goes out like a lion with Evita, director Jamie Lloyd’s revival of the Tim Rice and Andrew Lloyd Webber musical starring Rachel Zegler reprising her Olivier Award-winning performance as Eva Perón. Previews start February 27 at the Winter Garden – at the moment the home of Lloyd’s magnificent Much Ado – with an opening night of March 25.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

This Note-Taking Pebble Ring Is so Simple, and I Love It

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (897 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos.
  • In this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity.
  • To buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos. That seems like it would be underwhelming, and the idea was ridiculed by some of Pebble’s fans when the product was first confirmed. But I’ve been wearing it for a few weeks, and folks: I love it.

In this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity. This is a ring with no heart rate sensors or even charging pins, just a microphone, a button to activate it, and a light to let you know that it’s working. The audio is processed on your device; no need to send anything to the cloud.

To buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone. I use an iPhone rather than an Android, which means I can’t use certain features like setting timed reminders or connecting to Beeper, but it’s still an incredibly useful little device. The Index has no charger, since it uses a disposable battery that Pebble estimates will last about two years.

According to recent reports, the simplest way to use the Index is to wear it on your index finger (hence the name, get it?) and press the button with your thumb. Speak a quick note while holding the button in, and the ring will flash to let you know it got the message. A moment later, you’ll get a notification saying that it added (whatever you said) to your “Notes to self” note.

According to recent reports, to take this further, you can create different notes and ask the ring to add what you say to a specific note. You can also double-click the button to ask a question. The answer will appear in the notification you get on your phone or watch a moment later. (The ring does not speak to you.).

Sources indicate that all the notes you leave yourself appear as plain text in the Pebble app, fully editable. If you tap on each one, you can see a timestamp from when you left the note, and you can replay the voice recording if the transcription doesn’t make sense. (Why is there a “pencil sharp pepper” on my packing list? Ohh, that’s a pencil sharpener.) You can also add notes by typing them, which I find useful when starting a to-do list or a packing list.

According to recent reports, it’s incredible how useful a simple timestamped note can be. I used to do something similar with my “notes to self” chat in Signal, but the Index makes it even easier since I won’t get distracted by opening my phone. For example, I make a note on the Index whenever I take a medication, so that tomorrow morning I will be able to check whether I already took, say, a long-acting allergy pill. (You do not want to accidentally double up on those.).

There’s one thing that, for years, I wished for a simple tool to help me do. It’s trivial, which makes it extra frustrating that I have not been able to find a good solution. I would simply like to note when I leave for a road trip, and when I start and end each stop. This way I can tell how long the driving took as a portion of the whole trip, and how long my stops tend to be so I can strategy them better next time.

It has been revealed that you’d think this would be easy, but every existing tool drove me nuts in a different way. Stopwatches only store a single number, so I can’t break down how long each stop was—and if I miss a button press, I’m screwed. Sending myself a Signal text is probably my best option, but if I’ve just parked my car after three hours of driving, the second I pick up my phone I’m going to see all the notifications that arrived while I was on the road, and I’ll forget to actually send that text.

But this is exactly what the Index does well. I don’t even need to open my phone or look at my watch. Pressing the button with my thumb means I can do this one-handed without having a microphone always listening. (It’s also a great way to jot down the random things I think of while driving.).

Industry observers note that the Index worked perfectly for my travel log, and I even used it for a workout after I got to my hotel room that night. I’d do 10 pushups, then tell the ring “add 10 pushups to my workout.” I’d do 20 crunches, and add that as well. I left the workout note open on my phone and could glance over and see what I had already done, since my messages got added to the note as I went.

Sources indicate that I didn’t need a workout app for any of this, or a special-purpose travel app. I can just leave myself a dang note, and the note-taking app can remember when I left the note and, if I choose, play back exactly how I said it. It’s gloriously simple. Good job, Pebble.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps.
  • Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable owners to generate nonconsensual nude images.
  • According to the updated rules, apps that allow customers to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps. Here are the details.

Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable owners to generate nonconsensual nude images.

According to the updated rules, apps that allow customers to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.

Apple also warns that apps used primarily for pornographic content or the objectification of real people may be removed from the App Store without notice.

While definitely well-intended, Apple’s changes came amid growing reports of AI-powered nudify apps, which easily allow people to generate nonconsensual intimate images.

Two months before these changes, Apple removed an app that allowed users to create pornographic deepfakes of real people after WIRED reached out for comment, which in turn came one month after San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu demanded that Apple and Google remove several nudify apps from their app stores.

Apple also removed several apps following investigations by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), which published reports in January and April revealing that such apps were widely available on the App Store, sometimes even appearing in sponsored search results.

Throughout these investigations, Apple has maintained that nudify apps have always been prohibited under its App Review Guidelines, and that it proactively rejects and removes apps that violate its policies, including those flagged through user reports.

Apple, of course, is not alone in this challenge, with Google facing similar criticism over their availability on the Play Store, and Meta coming under scrutiny for allowing developers to advertise these apps on Facebook and Instagram, as highlighted in the WIRED report mentioned above.

Which brings us to today’s report from The Guardian.

According to The Guardian’s exclusive report, “three Senate Democrats sent letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms.”.

Sources indicate that A trio of US Senators say Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery. They also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

The senators, namely Ron Wyden of Oregon, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Ben Luján of New Mexico, claim that in addition to failing to remove these apps, the companies may actually be profiting from their distribution and promotion.

Commenting on the letter, both Google and Meta remarked they prohibit such apps or their promotion and work to detect and remove violations from their platforms, broadly echoing what Apple has repeatedly stated when reached for comment in the past over these same issues.

However, Wyden’s office argues that simply reaffirming, or in Apple’s case, updating these policies, means little if the companies continue to struggle to enforce them.

Keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, noted that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he added.

In its latest investigation, published just last month, TTP found 135 apps capable of generating nude or pornographic imagery on the App Store and the Play Store, using accounts registered to 13-year-old boys.

Additionally, researchers found that even accounts configured with parental controls were able to download these apps without requiring parental approval.

Despite Apple and Google removing the apps identified in the investigation, The Guardian noted that these apps continued to work on devices where they had already been installed.

Now, Senator Wyden warns that Congress may need to step in if the companies fail to do a better job of cracking down on these apps.

To read The Guardian’s full report, follow this link.

Industry observers note that enhancement, 8:40 p.m. ET: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple said:.

“We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for consumers. A number of the apps in the TTP report are mainstream photo and video editing tools with legitimate, widely used functionality, and do not have nudification or deepfake capabilities. We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process — a malicious tactic known as bait-and-switch. We previously removed 28 of the apps referenced in this report before it was shared with us and have taken action on the remaining apps found to violate our rules. The report also relies on testing from older software that does not reflect current Apple safety features, including expanded protections for teens and parental controls in Screen Time that give families the ability to block kids and teens from downloading apps rated above their age.”.

Expanding on the safety features mentioned in its statement, Apple noted that teens aged 13 through 17 now have certain protections enabled by default, including web content filters, even if their parents haven’t configured any restrictions, and pointed to ⁠this support article for more information.

The manufacturer added that children under 13 are required to use Child Accounts, and that the report relied on its previous 17+ age rating system, which was replaced last year with a more granular system that includes 13+, 16+, and 18+ ratings.

Just curious. Why doesn't someone from Apple try out the app before approving it, rather than approving it and waiting until people complain? I know there are many thousands of apps on the App store. But given that Apple makes money off most of these apps, it could surely afford to hire a staff charged with reviewing submitted apps to ensure compliance with the App store's guidelines and requirements before making them available in the App store. What am I missing here?

Apple also noted that in its report, TTP counted apps depicting people in swimwear or lingerie, which the organization mentioned does not constitute nudification or, in itself, violate its guidelines.

Industry observers note that as for parental controls, Apple explained that, although apps that exceed a child’s configured age restrictions won’t appear in curated App Store sections, they can still be found through search, allowing children to request permission to download them through Ask to Buy. Without parental approval, the download remains blocked.

According to recent reports, apple added that Ask to Buy is supposed to require parental approval even for purchases made using gift card balances, including subscriptions. The tech giant remarked that if a purchase didn’t trigger an approval request, that would be unexpected behavior, and that it is investigating further.

According to recent reports, update, November 19, 4:00 p.m. ET: In response to Apple’s statement, TTP director Katie Paul reached out to 9to5Mac with the following comment:.

Apple’s statement on nudify apps sidesteps key concerns and leaves out key context. The company says it prohibits nudify apps but doesn’t address how its age rating system for apps contributes to the problem. TTP has shown how Apple relies on information provided by app developers to set age ratings—a self-reporting system that allows many nudify and pornographic apps to be misleadingly labeled a suitable for minors. Apple also continues to talk about removing nudify apps from the App Store, without mentioning that apps that are “removed” continue to be fully functional on people’s phones.

There are many questions about Apple’s policy on nudify apps that the statement fails to address. Apple has adopted a limited definition of “nudify.” The company defines nudify apps as capable of showing someone naked, not stripping them down to a bikini or lingerie. But the company also indicates it bans “creepy” and “nonconsensual intimate imagery.” What if an app is used to depict a woman in a bikini without her consent? We have asked Apple to clarify that and have not heard back.

It has been revealed that as for Apple’s comment that TTP relied on “older software,” that may refer to the fact that Apple rolled out latest child safety features in the fall. Our research was conducted in summer 2026. But many of Apple’s new features pertain to parent-supervised accounts on Apple, which have to be set up by a parent. Apple relies entirely on parents to go out of their way to locate and enable these settings. This raises obvious questions about how many people actually do this.

It’s also packing 32GB of RAM (which is probably a good reason the price is as high as it is, given the ongoing RAM crisis) and 1TB of storage, as well as a microSD card slot. It has a unique “chin” to the display (more on that in a moment) that actually helps with ergonomics, and there’s improved button feel and haptics over MSI’s prior models.

According to recent reports, while we’d have loved OLED (especially at this price point), the IPS panel here has a variable refresh rate for smoother gameplay, and 8-inches, is actually significant enough to get some work done in a pinch with a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse combo. In fact, because it’s running Windows 11, you also get the Xbox Full Screen Experience for a more console-like experience: The best of both worlds.

In a recent development, every once in a while, Instagram rolls out an update that addresses one of its users’ most longstanding requests. Today is one of those days.

As spotted by The Verge, Instagram head Adam Mosseri confirmed today that the app will finally let users edit a Story after publishing.

This means owners will be able to add stickers and drawings, fix typos or adjust text, and even change the music without having to delete the Story and publish it again, which would mean losing any views it had already received.

The catch is that people will only have 15 minutes after publishing a Story to make changes by tapping the ellipsis button at the bottom of the screen, and then selecting “Edit story.”.

Here’s Mosseri’s post announcing the news:.

A post shared by Adam Mosseri (@mosseri).

Today’s update is the latest in a series of changes Instagram has made this year to address longstanding user requests.

Back in March, the app introduced the ability to reorder photos and videos in a carousel after publishing. In April, it added an option to edit comments (also within 15 minutes of posting), and in June, it began letting people manually rearrange posts on their profile grid.

More recently, Instagram also brought its free Edits video editor to the Mac, with multi-track editing, advanced color grading tools, and 4K exports.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CAA chief Bryan Lourd is urging the full Congress to pass the No Fakes Act and deliver it to President Trump for signature, a move Lourd indicates would protect everyone, famous or not, from nonconsensual digital replicas of their voices and likenesses.

Sources indicate that in a guest essay published in today’s New York Times, Lourd writes, “The Senate and House should move quickly and deliver the bill to President Trump for signature. That would ensure Americans retain control of their images and voices in the A.I. era.”.

Industry observers note that the No Fakes Act was approved unanimously by the Senate Judiciary Committee in June, and, Lourd contends, there “is momentum to pass it through the full Congress before the end of the year.” He calles it “one of the few A.I. bills with true bipartisan support.” Watch on Deadline.

Hollywood, Lourd writes, “is not afraid of new technology.”.

“The objection from actors, musicians and other creators is to a world in which anyone can use their face or voice without permission,” he writes. “In fact, many artists are already embracing A.I. on their own terms. Some of them are making deals with companies that are creating their A.I. likenesses, with their consent.”.

Lourd poses the issue as not just for Hollywood. “A content creator learned on her honeymoon that a YouTube ad was using an A.I. version of her to sell erectile dysfunction supplements,” he writes. “Is all this legal? Right now, it’s an open question. But it shouldn’t be.”.

“Hollywood doesn’t need America’s leaders to devise a latest concept for new circumstances,” writes the chief executive and co-chairman of Creative Artists Agency. “We need them to extend and enforce the rules that already exist. The use of Americans’ faces, voices, performances and creative works is already subject to rules at the federal or state level that say, in short: You need to get permission, and you need to pay for the use.”.

“This principle has guided the entertainment industry for more than a century,” he continues. “Whether it can continue to protect Americans may be decided in the coming weeks. The No Fakes Act would create a federal prohibition on creating nonconsensual digital replicas of any person’s voice or likeness — famous or not.”.

In a recent development, the No Fakes Act, Lourd indicates, “would apply a tried-and-true formula to the A.I. era: control, consent and compensation. It would set a uniform federal standard to replace outdated, ill-fitting state laws, many of them written with an analog world in mind. Its supporters include all sides of the table: SAG-AFTRA, the union representing actors and other performers; the Motion Picture Association, representing the studios; and tech companies including IBM, Google and OpenAI.”.

Earlier this month, Lourd told Deadline’s Dominic Patten, that the issues around AI are “about the fundamental relationship between technological progress and creative rights, and who determines the value of creative work, who decides how that work is used, and whether creators will share in the opportunities AI creates.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses.
  • That might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code.
  • Website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all customers, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses. Now there's something upcoming. You can also build interactive websites from your notebooks.

That might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code. But it gives you another way to look at your material and to get insights from it. Here's how it works, what you could potentially do with it, and how impressively it worked when I put it to the test on some early 20th-century Irish literature.

Website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all customers, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app. You won't see a website option in the Studio panel alongside Audio Overview, Reports, Quiz, and the rest; instead, you type something along the lines of "make me a website" in the prompt box.

According to recent reports, to make a website, you need sources, so I set Gemini Notebook to collect information about James Joyce's 1914 collection of short stories, Dubliners. As I studied Dubliners many years ago (I highly recommend it), I was hoping I'd spot any AI errors and hallucinations, and be able to properly assess the quality of Gemini Notebook's analysis.

With a suitable amount of information absorbed into the AI brain, I got Gemini Notebook to make me a website. Google doesn't give too much official guidance here, but states you should add "a description of what you want to build for work or study," so if you have a particular style or angle in mind, include it.

Here was my prompt: "Build a website using all the sources and information collected so far. Make it an interactive guide to the individual stories in Dubliners, as well as the overarching themes and context. I want to use it as a study aid to explore different aspects of the story collection.".

Sources indicate that the finished website pops up in the Studio panel, and in my case it took around five minutes to put something together from 26 different sources. Click on the website, and it opens in a upcoming window—you can use it from there, open it in a separate tab, or download the code to your computer.

I was honestly impressed by how much Gemini Notebook managed to pack into a single website: I got plot summaries, analysis, critical context, and some of the main themes and motifs outlined. There was an interactive quiz at the bottom of the page to test my knowledge, and even a graphic I could click through to reveal different elements of how the stories fit together.

Industry observers note that everything was well laid out and functional, albeit with the standard "sheen" you get from anything made by AI (which tends to always pick the same colors and fonts). I wouldn't have necessarily thought that I needed a website if I was still studying Dubliners today, but I can definitely see how it would have helped.

In a recent development, for something like my project, a website really works well as a study aid, since it offers a different way of interrogating the information. You can already do that in the main chat, and with tools such as the audio and video overviews, but this is different. It's a bit like having a mini-Wikipedia focused just on whatever you're researching.

The interactive elements that are included—so in my example, I could click from story to story, and theme to theme, within the same page—make a site more engaging than a standard report document and a static wall of text, and should help the information stick if you're trying to study it.

I can also see how this might be useful for sharing data with others. Maybe you need to analyze monthly report figures, or you want to chart how your organization has developed a product over time—perhaps an interactive website will relay that information in a more compelling way than a slide deck or PDF.

Maybe you have a notebook stuffed with details of a massive family vacation. Putting together a website through Gemini Notebook would give your family a hub that they could use to easily check up on the details of the trip—where you're going and when, what you'll see there, what they need to pack, and so on. Another idea might be a family tree, if you have ancestry data and sources packed together in a notebook. Putting together a website would be a great way to visualize it, and, again, it's something you could share with relatives. If there were updates to the data you've collected, you could generate a upcoming website.

Industry observers note that bear in mind that you can do a lot with your prompt. My website turned out the way it did because that's what I asked for, and if you need more interactivity or specific types of sections, then you can ask. Based on my follow-up prompts, you can also specify colors and certain layout choices, though it's not quite a full-scale website builder.

According to recent reports, it looks like these sites are single-page creations, though they do have interactive elements and sections that change as you click around. It might be better to think of them as mini apps rather than sites. As of yet, there's no built-in option for publishing a site online or sharing it with others, so you need to download the HTML and do that manually.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.
  • In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue remarked Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a latest interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month. Here are the details.

Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.

In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue remarked Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.

Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, however, has now offered a more concrete figure, revealing that the service reaches over 50 million unique listeners every month:.

We were never, you know, delusional enough to assume we were going to get a huge audience overnight. We’d have to build it like anyone else would have to build anything. But we’ve just got to a point in our 11 years on where we now, overall, reach over 50 million unique listeners a month, which is a really large number for us, and it’s growing exponentially and really fast.

The revelation came in a wide-ranging interview published today with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, where Lowe discussed Apple Music Radio’s early struggles, its approach to supporting emerging artists, and why human curation remains central to the service.

When discussing the early days at Apple Music, Lowe recalled:.

Recent findings suggest that when we started the radio here, I didn’t have access or opportunity with a lot of the artists that I built relationships with from the BBC because we were unproven. And I came over here thinking, “Well, I’ve got Jimmy Iovine over here, and I’ve got Apple over here and I feel unstoppable, and who’s not going to want to come and launch this thing with us?” But it was kind of crickets… As upsetting as that was at the time, two good things came out of it. Number one, it snapped me back into the reality force field of building something from scratch. And number two, it made us focus really clearly and in a big way on fresh and emerging artists.

He also mentioned some of the first artists Apple Music Radio supported, including Billie Eilish with “Ocean Eyes,” Khalid with American Teen, and Bryson Tiller with his first song.

At the time, Lowe noted, these artists were just getting started, and supporting emerging talent became a defining part of Apple Music Radio’s approach, one that continues to this day:.

According to recent reports, the really cool number is on our radio network. We played — this year alone — over 6,500 individual artists, which is not a commercial radio model. [Other radio networks’] playlists are very small, and the amount of plays is very great. Our playlist is gigantic. We play a lot of different artists, and over half of those 6,500 artists we’ve played in one year are newly introduced or emerging. So, think about 3,300 artists, roughly, getting played, who may be on their first song, their first EP, their first album…It’s proof of concept. It’s great.

Still on the subject of the early days at Apple Music, Lowe mentioned “it was very clear [from the start] that that was very important to everybody who was responsible for bringing Apple Music to life,” adding that “serving artists and the artistic community in a way that is of most value and of most service” still drives “a lot of the decision-making” at the platform.

When the conversation turned to Apple Music’s recent rebranding, which introduced a upcoming logo physically created using sound waves from a composition by Fred again.., Lowe stated he couldn’t speak to the decisions behind it, but stressed the human element and the creative process that went into it:.

We could have created that in a way that could utilize all of the tech available. We could type that into a prompt. But at the end of the day, seeing how it’s made is so much more additionally inspiring than just seeing it. It speaks to, I think, what we try to do here, which is, we love the process of what we do, and the result is a byproduct of getting to do it and loving to do it.

The glitch of algorithms also came up when Lowe discussed Apple Music’s approach to music discovery, with the executive emphasizing the importance of human curation over automated recommendations:.

Recent findings suggest that well, we don’t want to say that too loudly, because someone could be like, “Wait a minute, we could cut costs here? Man, how did we not think of that!” Look, I mean, jokes aside, we’ve been incredibly fortunate, and I’ve been incredibly fortunate to take that step from the BBC into a company and to work with people that value exactly what it is you’re describing: this idea of place and this experience of sharing things with each other, and how meaningful it is when someone shares a record with you and it comes with context. It’s a gift….

Watermelon Pictures and the Film Committee at Media City Qatar have revealed a planned strategic partnership to develop and co-produce a slate of films telling stories from the Global South.

The partnership marks a significant expansion into larger-scale, mainstream production for Watermelon Pictures.

Badie Ali and Hamza Ali released their Chicago-based production and distribution company in 2024, with a mission to amplify Palestinian and other under-represented voices.

Sources indicate that until now, the organization has focused mainly on distribution, with recent releases including The Voice of Hind Rajab, El Sett, Who Killed Alex Odeh? and American Doctor. Related Stories News Egyptian Music Star Mohamed Mounir Gets Biopic - Doha Industry Days News 'Al Hayba' Star Taim Hasan To Play Syrian Whistleblower Farid Al-Madhhan In Neon-Backed 'Caesar' Biopic.

Its cofounders recently signaled to Deadline that they were working on a development slate, without going into detail. Watch on Deadline.

The strategic partnership aims to combine Qatar’s infrastructure and resources as it seeks to grow the film and TV sector at home and regionally, and Watermelon’s access to leading talent, established distribution infrastructure, and understanding of what resonates with audiences.

“When we founded Watermelon Pictures, our vision was to bring powerful stories to the major screen with an unwavering commitment to authenticity,” remarked Watermelon Pictures cofounder Badie Ali.

“Our partnership with the Film Committee at Media City Qatar is a major step toward realizing that promise, allowing us to tell these stories on a larger scale while remaining true to the people and places at their heart.”.

Under the partnership, the parties would aim to shoot projects substantially in Qatar or structure them as Qatari co-productions.

They would also seek to involve Doha-based post-production companies and help eligible projects access the Qatar Screen Production Incentive (QSPI), creating opportunities for local crews, businesses, and creative talent while strengthening Qatar’s position as an international production hub.

Recent findings suggest that “Through this partnership, we want to give filmmakers the resources to tell stories rooted in their communities and bring them to audiences around the world. We also want the films we support to create work for crews and businesses in Qatar and give them experience they can carry into their next production,” stated Hassan Al Thawadi, Chairman of the Film Committee at Media City Qatar.

In a recent development, the Film Committee and Watermelon Pictures will jointly identify projects for the initial slate. The proposed partnership is subject to definitive agreements and the required approvals, with projects to be considered individually. More details on specific projects are soon to be confirmed.

In a recent development, “Too many compelling stories and perspectives, including those of Arab and Muslim communities, have historically been underrepresented in mainstream cinema. We see an enormous opportunity to change that. Our planned slate will span genres, challenge perceptions, and, above all, entertain. Our ambition isn’t simply to create space in the industry. It’s to compete at its highest level,” stated Watermelon Pictures cofounder Hamza Ali.

The announcement of the planned partnership was made during the Film Committee’s Doha Industry Days, running from November 19 to 21 within the framework of the Doha Film Festival.

This time-hopping survival drama is about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive—the extent of which we only learn about via flashbacks from the present day, where the events of 19 months spent in the wild continue to resonate. There are ambiguous teases of the supernatural here (much more ambiguous than in The Body), but there's plenty of human-level horror as well. The show explores the nasty things we get up to when in survival mode (whether trapped in the wilds, stuck with other teenagers—or god forbid both at once), while also cynically (but accurately) positing that there's a huge difference between the version of the past we talk about and the one that really happened. Stream Yellowjackets on Paramount+.

It has been revealed that situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It swiftly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, and the ways in which we'll do just about anything when survival is on the line. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

Sources indicate that when pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

It has been revealed that juicy import Elite follows a group of working-class friends who earn scholarships to Las Encinas, a fictional private school that is, in the show’s universe, the most exclusive in Spain. What they find there is snobbery, mystery, murder, and lots and lots of sex (between and among characters of various sexual orientations and numerical groupings). The smart, wonderfully trashy show ran for a shocking (in our modern streaming era) eight seasons, with a couple of regional remakes. There's no supernatural stuff here, but plenty of dark deeds done with youthful vigor. Stream Elite on Netflix.

A teenager, Mae (Madeleine Arthur), is discovered by the side of the road with weird religious symbols carved into her skin. The hospital psychiatrist who treats her (Emily Deschanel) takes pity on, and interest in, Mae, deciding to take her in while arrangements can be made for a more permanent home for the cult escapee. Mae is, after all, level-headed and quiet, and couldn't possibly be any trouble. Hoo boy, yeah, that turns out to be a bad call on the good doctor's part. Stream Devil in Ohio on Netflix.

In a recent development, A different type of blasphemy at play here, in that Joan Lindsay's novel was already adapted brilliantly by Peter Weir in 1975, in a film often referred to as the greatest to come out of Australia. And yet, this Natalie Dormer-lead take is an achievement in its own right, the extended running time of a miniseries offering up more time to sit with the story's deliberately ineffable mysteries. Dormer plays Hester Appleyard, headmistress of a school for young ladies in the Australian bush. It's going well until a Valentine's Day picnic to the title's Hanging Rock sees three students and a governess disappear, impossibly, without a trace, bringing about the slow unravelling of pretty much everyone left behind. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on Prime Video and Tubi.

According to recent reports, mariam (Andria Tayeh) is brutally bullied by the cool clique at her private school in this Jordanian import, a high school drama that's both universal and distinctly Muslim in character. Fed up, Mariam convinces a couple of similarly outcast friends to join forces with her in a revenge plot that promptly gets out of hand. The show deals with Jordanian-style patriarchy head-on, without drawing any easy conclusions about its characters—Mariam catfishes one of her bullies and convinces her to send a revealing picture, one that she immediately posts, exploiting the very same repressive cultural elements that she claims to deplore. It's a smart, realist drama with soapy elements and nothing by way of the supernatural, but it's still a very sharp picture of the extremely cutthroat nature of high school life. Stream AlRawabi School for Girls on Netflix.

In a recent development, peyton List stars as Maddie, a teenager in small-town Wisconsin for whom her death is very much just the beginning. Stuck in a high school in the afterlife (because hell is definitely for children), she goes on a journey to solve her own murder while uncovering secrets and lies in both worlds. It all sounds a bit grim, but the show has a sense of fun about it: While Maddie does develop the ability to communicate with the living, her world is populated by ghost teens from various eras and generations, with customs, mores, and cliques having developed in ghost high school just as in our world. Stream School Spirits on Paramount+.

The newly introduced Girigo app, claiming to grant wishes, sounds like harmless fun. Except, of course, that the things that teenagers want aren't always beneficent, and the app has already been the conduit for some incredibly dark deeds by the time it gets into the hands of the five high schoolers who find themselves caught in a Ring-like web of shamanistic horror and death countdowns. This is why we tell you to put your phones down once in a while... Stream If Wishes Could Kill on Netflix.

Four one-time best friends reunite at Rosewood High School a year after the disappearance of the leader of their little clique, all having received threatening messages from the mysterious "A," who knows everything they did last summer...and pretty much all the rest of the time. Shoplifting, parents having affairs, students hooking up with teachers—you name it, it's happening in town, and A knows it all. After the prime suspect turns up dead, the girls are caught in the killer's web while trying to keep their secrets hidden. If seven juicy seasons and three A's aren't enough for you, there are three spin-offs. Stream Pretty Little Liars on Hulu and HBO Max.

#51174. Unit-testing in the Ü programming language

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1578 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Github ↗ Open Full Page

Unit-testing in the Ü programming language

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1578 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Now Ü has built-in unit-testing functionality.
  • halt is used for handling test failures, but it’s recommended to use some macro (like assert) which is able to print into stderr, what exactly went wrong.
  • Running such tests is possible via simple command test supported now by the Ü build system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Now Ü has built-in unit-testing functionality. Writing a unit-test is as simple as this:.

halt is used for handling test failures, but it’s recommended to use some macro (like assert) which is able to print into stderr, what exactly went wrong.

Running such tests is possible via simple command test supported now by the Ü build system.

Recent findings suggest that fn_test is just a special syntax, which allows defining a unit-test function. Unit-test functions are almost like regular ones, but there are small differences in the way how they are built. They get internal encoded names, so that it’s not possible to reference a unit-test (call it manually). They always have external linkage and unit-test functions defined in imported files get comdat, so that they are deduplicated. Also unit-test functions are marked with special metadata, so that it’s possible to identify them and process later.

Recent findings suggest that what happens later is more interesting. While the Ü build system links regular build targets, unit-test functions are internalized and thus optimized-out, so that they are not present in result machine code. But it also creates executables containing unit-tests for each build target. This is done by launching the Ü compiler with special flag, which enables building of a table where all unit-test functions are listed. Then the result machine code containing this table is linked against a special library, which knows how to use it.

Industry observers note that how this unit-testing library is implemented? The simplest implementation would be just to loop over all tests in the unit-tests table and to call them. Such approach is fine, but only in cases where all unit-tests are successful. As long as at least one unit-test fails, the whole unit-testing process crashes and thus no further unit-tests can be run and their status can’t be reported. So, some way of failure-recovery is necessary.

Recent findings suggest that languages like C++ often use exceptions for reporting test failures. This approach works, generally, even if it isn’t ideal. Rust has no exceptions, but it has stack unwinding, which is usually executed on panic being triggered. It functions almost exactly like unwinding in C++ happening after an exception is thrown. But Ü has no exceptions or even unwinding. It was a design decision not to implement it. Exceptions make things harder by obscuring control-flow and breaking local reasoning. Unwinding isn’t implemented, since it’s again breaks local reasoning and requires writing code in an unwinding-safe way, which is hard to do.

Industry observers note that so, Ü needed a way to report test failures in some other way. First I tried experimenting with setjmp/longjmp approach and signal handlers. This is already not a good way of doing things, since recovering after a failure using longjmp doesn’t allow calling destructors, which leads to memory leaks, files left in opened state or even perpetually-locked mutexes. But I thought that it’s a lesser evil to use them rather than having no proper way of handling failures in unit-tests at all. I did a couple of experiments with such approach. setjmp with longjmp executed in signal handler worked as intended on Linux systems. But on Windows it didn’t work as expected. And it’s not clear whether it’s correct to call longjmp from a signal handler, C standard doesn’t describe this clearly. So, eventually I abandoned this approach.

There was last alternative - use proper per-process isolation. It allows handling failures gracefully, if a process crashes, it (almost always) frees resources associated with it. I experimented with running each unit-test in its separate process. This did work well on Linux, but with some noticeable overhead (roughly 1ms for starting each child process and waiting for it to finish). On Windows it did work too, but order of magnitudes slower than on Linux - with 15ms overhead for each process (slightly less if antivirus-scanning is disabled in system settings). So, it works, but it may be too slow if many unit-tests (hundreds to thousands) are present.

Recent findings suggest that in the end I decided to use a more tricky approach. A separate process is started for running unit-tests. Many unit-tests are run sequentially inside it, as long as no test failure/crash is detected. In case of test failure or other crash, the parent process restarts the child to continue running tests. A block of shared memory is used between the parent and child processes to track already finished tests or tests which have been started, but failed. Since restarting a child process isn’t cheap, there is a limit on how many times it can be done, like 32 times. So, only up to 32 failed test-cases can be reported, which isn’t ideal, but mostly fine. It’s enough work for a programmer to identify what went wrong and to fix failed tests.

Each unit-tests executable creates a child process for running actual tests. On Unix fork call is used for that. On Windows a unit-tests executable runs itself using CreateProcessW with a special command-line flag to indicate, that it’s a child instance.

Using process-based tests isolation has one more advantage. Not only halt usages are caught as test failures. Any other process crash can be detected and reported, this includes access violation, integer division by zero, stack overflow and others. This allows catching failures caused by incorrectly-written unsafe code, incorrectly-used external code, infinite recursion and similar cases not handled directly by Ü safety mechanisms. The only thing which is (for now) can’t be handled are deadlocks, which are tricky to detect (it’s unclear whether there is a deadlock or just long computation).

The approach with running unit-tests in a separate process has one significant disadvantage. Debugging failed tests (with a debugger) isn’t that easy, since debuggers (usually) don’t debug child processes. As a workaround for this issue a small trick has been implemented - a unit-tests executable detects if a debugger is present, and if it’s the case, no child process is spawned and all tests are run in the current process instead.

Sources indicate that the Ü build system has test command, which runs all unit-tests. But there are some caveats in it. It’s assumed, that the target triple specified for a project is compatible with host target triple. In other words, it’s assumed, that running test executables can be possible on host system. It’s not true in case of cross-compilation, like if building a project for Windows on Linux machine or building a project for iOS from OS X. But even if cross-compilation is performed, tests are built anyway. They can be still useful, if one finds a way to run them (somehow) on target system, even if running them on host using the test command isn’t possible.

It has been revealed that unit-test functions are always built. There is no way to skip building them. It’s done in order to be able to fix compilation errors in them as rapidly as possible, if code on which they depend has been changed. It’s always good to fix compilation errors early, rather then to perform such forgotten fixes later.

Unit-test executables are generated for each build target by-default. It’s done in this way to encourage usage of unit-testing. Building unit-tests is pretty cheap. For each build target its unit-tests executable is linked from the same bitcode files obtained by compiling target’s source files, which are later used for linking this build target. So, no double work is performed. Linking unit-test executables and generating machine code for them isn’t free, but it’s almost free if no unit-tests at all are present or if there are only a few of them testing only a small part of the target’s codebase (dead code is eliminated before generating machine code).

One may ask, why using special syntax with fn_test? Why having separate support of unit-testing in the build system? Many other languages don’t have such built-in functionality, but unit-testing in them still can be used. And why unit-test building and linking is turned-on by-default?

According to recent reports, the answer is: friction reduction. Creating unit-tests in Ü is as easy as writing a fn_test function and running the test command of the build system. No extra setup is necessary. No thirdparty unit-testing framework needs to be integrated. No separate custom steps are needed for building and launching unit-tests. With such low friction there is little to no reason not to write unit-tests, since it’s that easy. And since unit-test linking is turned-on by-default, there is no danger to forget by mistake that no unit-tests are actually run.

It’s assumed, that such low-friction may encourage writing unit-tests. And more unit-tests means better overall quality of the result software written in Ü.

After unit-testing functionality has been implemented, some unit-tests have been added in various places of Ü codebase. This includes parts of Compiler1 and the build system. And they seem to work well. A lot of functionality remains uncovered by such unit-tests, primary because it has been already written and debugged properly and because there are other ways for testing it. But I expect, that new unit-tests may be added for new pieces of functionality in future.

In a recent development, there is no drastic increase in build times caused by linking unit-test executables. It’s not entirely free, but fast enough in order to not care about it. And if in some rare case it creates some undesirable slow-down, one can still disable unit-tests for a particular build target.
