Industry observers note that ice storms cause long outages because several exposures act together. Ice adds weight to conductors, hardware and structures. Wind pushes on the larger iced surface. Trees and limbs bend into the line and add impact and uneven load. Conductors may also gallop and lose clearance. This paper explains how these loads combine and why the complete line must be assessed, not a single component. It reviews a monitored winter test of three conductor systems. It also summarizes utility records from a major regional ice storm. Finally, it outlines how to choose corridors, plan restoration and keep crews and the public safe around covered conductors.

  • The last day to use the To Do apps is June 30, 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft is saying goodbye to its task management service To Do, including the Mac and iOS apps. Here’s what users need to know.

The last day to use the To Do apps is June 30, 2027. That date also applies to Windows, Android, and the web. The underlying service and sync support will retire later, according to Microsoft’s support document.

“Microsoft To Do is retiring,” Microsoft explains. “For work or school accounts, Microsoft Planner will be the destination for managing personal work tasks alongside assigned work. The updated My tasks experience begins rolling out in December 2026.”.

On the Mac, you can use Planner on the web or in Teams. Microsoft explicitly says it has no aims for a native Mac app.

It has been revealed that you can still see your existing To Do tasks in Planner through June 30, but your tasks and lists won’t carry over. Microsoft aims to offer an export option before the apps retire.

Planner doesn’t support personal Microsoft accounts however. If that’s how you use To Do, you’ll need to pick another task manager, even if you pay for Microsoft 365 Personal or Family, according to the organization.

Sources indicate that the June shutdown will end a run of just over a decade for To Do on Apple platforms. Microsoft bought the company behind Wunderlist in 2015 and released the first iPhone preview of To Do in April 2017.

Recent findings suggest that looking for a proper replacement? Apple’s built-in Reminders app can keep lists in sync between Apple devices, including a grocery list you share with family through iCloud.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft has been trying to make Teams as the super app for some time now, as Planner is integrated into Teams. Teams is one of the prime examples of why super apps are terrible, with a bloated, web app-like experience.

If you liked To Do because it worked across platforms, Todoist has apps for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Windows, and Android.

According to recent reports, does this sunsetting affect you? Were you a Wunderlist user back in the day? Share your thoughts in the comments.

Recent findings suggest that “We’re bringing task management experiences together across Microsoft 365 to make it easier for customers to manage individual tasks and team looks. As part of this transition, Microsoft To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027, with work and school experiences coming together in Microsoft Planner. Existing integrations across Microsoft 365, including Outlook and Teams, will also be updated to work with Planner. We recognize this change will affect customers differently, particularly those using personal Microsoft accounts, and we’re committed to helping them prepare. Customers will be able to export their To Do data before retirement, and we’ll share additional guidance to support the transition.”.

Breaking: I tested the Xreal Aura glasses for 2 weeks — amazing displays and immersive spatial computing let down by a lack of apps

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Xreal and Google's first foray into XR glasses is a fascinating look at the future of AR and VR devices.
  • According to recent reports, why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you.
  • For quite awhile I have firmly believed that smart glasses are the next device that will evolve the future of computing, much like the iPhone heralded the next 20 years of tech progression.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Xreal and Google's first foray into XR glasses is a fascinating look at the future of AR and VR devices. But that also means you're prototyping something that will get better, but maybe not yet.

According to recent reports, why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

For quite awhile I have firmly believed that smart glasses are the next device that will evolve the future of computing, much like the iPhone heralded the next 20 years of tech progression. And this is despite the current "pervert glasses" backlash.

I am fascinated by the sudden influx of AR and XR glasses that offer immersive environments and while also looking "normal." I've already tried Meta VR Glasses and Snap Specs, but neither are actually available for everyone yet. The Google, Qualcomm and Xreal collaboration Aura glasses are.

All three glasses could be considered VR-lite, but I think they're about finding a use between AI glasses and wearing a full headset.

In that way, the Auras are the escaped experiment worth investigating. Following the Samsung Galaxy XR headset, these are just the second device to run Google's Android XR platform natively.

This first stab at an XR headset that I think most people will want is impressive and a great example of what Android XR could be, but it also means you're the guinea pig with all that implies.

90g (glasses)265g (compute puck).

Xreal S1 andQualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite Platform.

Recent findings suggest that right when the Aura released on November 17, I put together some early impressions of the glassese. For the most part, my thoughts haven't changed. But after using the glasses more, some plusses and minuses have solidified.

In a recent development, I am not an advocate for VR as it currently works with bulky, isolating headsets. However, I can still be impressed virtual reality experiences.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Industry observers note that the Xreal Aura provides that with 6DoF spatial computing. The two temple cameras and the nose bridge camera enable pinch gesture controls and you can always use the puck as trackpad, which I defaulted to more often that not.

In a recent development, the pinch controls work well. Occasionally the hitbox was a hair off but I didn't notice lag when I adjusted. I will note that in darker environments, it didn't always work, which isn't totally surprising but something to know.

Out of the box, the Auras come with a variety of mixed-reality experiences, from a VR tour of the Galapagos, to some games and a 360 version of Google Maps that is a delight to explore.

VR enthusiasts will find the 70-degree field of view limiting but I wasn't bothered by it. Watching movies feels like you're in a theater for yourself, and extending my desktop workspace was seamless via the wired accessory cable (or wireless for some devices).

These might be the best displays Xreal has made to date. I tested the refreshed Xreal One Pro Plus a couple of weeks ago and thought it was an improvement, and now the Aura is taking it even further.

Xreal lists the resolution of the Aura's as 1,920 x 1,200 per eye (1200p). It makes for sharp images, especially in games and media. It feels premium.

The color gamut isn't robust and the Aura doesn't offer HDR like the One Pro Plus, but if you don't need that level of display detail, these look good. Plus, with 1200 nits of brightness, the display can handle a number of settings. And the electrochromic dimming gets pretty dark, meaning you should feel more immersed.

In a recent development, personally, I have never had great luck reading text as is on AR glasses, and while the Aura's are better, you may find text blurry. Fortunately, you can zoom in, which helps.

One advantage the Xreal Aura glasses have over Meta's VR Glasses and the Snap Specs is the built-in Google ecosystem. Snap and Meta have both promised that they're building up their developer connections to create more apps for their glasses, but Google's slew of in-house designs and third-party apps is already robust.

On the productivity side, you've got the entire Google suite from Docs and Drive to your calendar and Gmail. Plus, there's the Google Play Store with normal phone games and a small but growing number of XR-specific apps.

Moving forward, as Android XR grows, this will be what sets the Aura and future Android XR devices apart from Snap and Meta.

Industry observers note that here's the rub: you don't really need XR glasses yet. Xreal's own lineup of AR glasses are already great for productivity, gaming and watching content by connecting to your laptop, mini PC, phone or gaming device.

Because of that, the flaws do stand out a bit more.

If we're thinking of the Aura as VR-lite, especially compared to the Meta VR Glasses, then the biggest missing component for the Xreal Aura glasses is games.

Yes, I did try Demeo, which was fun, and HoloChess, which felt like the Star Wars version of chess. But from what I could tell, there aren't many native XR/VR games on the Play Store, while the Meta Quest Store has hundreds, and Meta promised at least 75 launch titles specifically designed for the VR glasses next year.

You can play 2D games on the Play Store, which I did with some games I already have on my account. Xreal is selling its own first-party controller made with GameSir, but you can use any Bluetooth controller. Again, you can connect other Xreal glasses to your phone, laptop, or gaming device with a controller as well.

It's not clear how long it'll take native Android XR experiences to catch up to Meta, but for now, Meta has the lead.

Xreal rates the battery life of the Aura puck between three and four hours. I found that to be pretty accurate. In my testing watching an hour-long YouTube video and then playing some games for about 20 minutes knocked the battery life from 100% to about 80%.

I debated putting this as a flaw because I'm not sure if you want to keep these glasses on for more than three hours. Perhaps that is the sweet spot. Still, for anything longer, you'll need to recharge.

That mentioned, heat becomes a concern. The puck can get warm, but it does include a fan to dissipate heat. Surprisingly, the glasses can get quite warm, especially in the area that runs across your forehead.

Industry observers note that general use seemed okay, but at one point I accidentally turned on screen recording and I could feel the glasses heating up. It never got laptop-panini levels of hot, but as the tech ages, I foresee this being a problem.

The Xreal Auras have just three cameras. Two on the temples and one on the nose bridge. As mentioned, I find the hand tracking pretty decent and pinch gestures work well.

It has been revealed that however, I've also worn the Meta VR Glasses, which have 6 external cameras and four internal ones. Fundamentally, Xreal adding seven more cameras would change the design of the glasses, which you can see in the ski-goggle look of Meta's forthcoming platform.

Still, eye tracking makes navigating the XR space better. And compared to Meta, where you can leave your hand on the table or in your lap and still use gesture controls, the three-camera Aura setup is more limiting.

The pushback is the puck trackpad, which I used most frequently. I am comfortable with trackpads and mice, and the puck is a nice midway point.

The puck is a mini-PC with glasses attached, but that doesn't make navigation the best without accessories or the trackpad.

If Xreal's next iteration can add eye tracking or even a couple more external cameras, the already good hand tracking would be even better.

I find the Xreal Aura glasses fascinating, and when its rivals finally launch, I think a latest space in the tech world will open up that is more than just pervert glasses and bulky headsets. Perhaps I've given these glasses more grace than future versions will deserve, but for a first go in this space, I'm excited by the potential.

For many, I'm not sure the $1,000+ price tag is cheap enough to dive in, but for the curious and the early adopters, this is a device of potential. It hints at what mixed reality wearables could be.

When I use the Aura, I get what it's supposed to be. It's the taste of a Vision Pro or Quest headset in a lighter, more comfortable package. Xreal has set the bar; it'll be up to everyone to see if they can raise it.

#51122. Tech Report: Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2384 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Linebender ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2384 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Linebender

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs, published 4.5 years ago.
  • The motivation to build GUI apps in Rust remains strong.
  • According to recent reports, adoption of Rust UI in the past few years has been slow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs, published 4.5 years ago. The world is different in many ways, but some of the advice there is still valid. There have been roughly 20 Rust GUI toolkits confirmed since that blog post (see 2026 survey), but also a recent rapid acceleration of interest in Rust GUI, fueled by AI.

The motivation to build GUI apps in Rust remains strong. Many shipping GUI apps suffer from poor performance, especially when built with cross-platform technology. GUI toolkits shipped by platforms have largely stagnated, and system vendors remain uninterested in solving the cross-platform problem, so Electron has grown in popularity. RAM remains expensive and the focus is shifting to mobile, so bloat has real consequences. Building high-performance UI in Rust is a practical alternative.

According to recent reports, adoption of Rust UI in the past few years has been slow. Few flagship apps use Rust for their UI. One of the most notable is the Zed editor, built on their own GPUI framework. It proves that shipping Rust UI is practical, and indeed, GPUI is emerging as a major choice for AI-driven rewrites, most notably Discord. My personal sense is that GPUI is well suited to the Zed use case, and shipping in a real project boosts its visibility and credibility quite a bit, but it’s not necessarily the ideal choice for more general purpose applications. Among other things, its 2D rendering engine is well suited to a text editor, but lacks full gradient support, blending, filters, and other features expected of a renderer in the same class as Vello or Skia.

According to recent reports, the reasons for slow adoption may be melting away. Writing Rust code is harder than languages more traditionally used for UI (TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift), and finding engineers skilled in both Rust and UI is challenging. But AI is changing the game. There’s evidence that the LLM cost of writing Rust code is not significantly higher than other languages, and there is reason to believe that in large codebases, Rust will be more maintainable because its type system helps enforce invariants. So if all languages have roughly the same cost, then why not go with one that has a dramatically better combination of safety and performance?

Recent findings suggest that for these reasons, Rust is rapidly becoming the language for AI rewrites of existing codebases. But there is still no consensus on the strategy for the UI layer. I predict there will be a small explosion of trying lots of different things.

My 2022 blog post had a large section on “native,” first pointing out that the term has no clear meaning, and more broadly pointing out that “native” UI toolkits are simply choices among many, and should be evaluated on the crucial quality criteria.

It has been revealed that I think this is largely still true, but it depends greatly on which platform is being targeted. Windows still has no clear native choice (see Microsoft Hasn’t Had a Coherent GUI Strategy Since Petzold) and on Mac there is a bit of fragmentation between AppKit and SwiftUI. However, SwiftUI has performance complications (see Michael Tsai blog from 2025) and so it is clearly possible to do better on the performance front.

According to recent reports, while desktop UI has remained stagnant, the situation on mobile is a bit different. Platforms continue to invest, and there are many fine details that are notable for an app to look and feel native. One very notable example is Liquid Glass on iOS – if you use UIKit or SwiftUI, you can get that with little effort, but apps built with cross-platform toolkits won’t quite seem right. In addition, making gesture recognition, scroll dynamics, and IME 100% match the platform are not yet fully solved problems.

In a recent development, thus, for mobile, an extremely viable path is to use the native toolkit for UI but do the common “business logic” in Rust. I’m not sure about the business logic, but for the UI, this is the decision that Shopify has made recently, abandoning React Native. I believe 1Password has this architecture. This is also the "Phoenix" strategy for Discord on mobile, while using GPUI on desktop.

Sources indicate that that noted, there's been considerable progress in trying to build mobile UI entirely in Rust. Below is a short screencast of the editor demo in android-view. You can see that a lot of IME functionality works, including swiping, moving the cursor by rolling the space bar, and deleting in semantic chunks. Not shown in the video below, but composition regions (needed for CJK) also work, and there's basic accessibility through AccessKit.

It has been revealed that one of the big unsolved problems as of the 2022 blog post was text layout. It is of course a hard problem to get right. I’m pleased to say that the ecosystem now has a good solution, in the form of Parley. It’s gotten there as a result of sustained investment from Google, Canva, and Dioxus (now Cognition), as well as contributions from the community. It seems to be used in the majority of newly introduced Rust UI toolkits. In addition, to help mitigate the risk of monoculture, Cosmic Text is a viable alternative.

AccessKit was just getting started in 2022, but is now solid infrastructure as well, and used by most UI toolkits. I should note, though, there is a difference between a good integration and a box ticking exercise. And there is more work to be done, for example to make rich text editing fully accessible. One other problem I'd like to see addressed is performance degradation when accessibility is enabled. This is a problem for egui in particular, as it has to build and diff a tree each animation frame, undercutting the benefits of its underlying immediate mode design.

In a recent development, one topic I talked about extensively in the 2022 blog post is leveraging the system compositor. This issue is even more pressing today, especially with the increased importance of video. You really want a video playing in a hardware accelerated layer when possible, and on low end devices it’s the only hope for getting smooth frame rates.

Sources indicate that there has been some progress, notably the subduction library, but it certainly isn’t commonly integrated into UI toolkits yet. To do it well is a challenging problem, as the capabilities provided by the platform vary widely. Ideally there’s a rich and high level interface, something like CALayer on Apple platforms, and polyfills to implement that interface as well as possible on other platforms. On Android, when the task is something simple, like overlaying some GUI controls on a video, it would use SurfaceFlinger layers, but when it involves more sophisticated compositing, it would run shaders on the GPU.

This is absolutely something we should build, ideally as a high quality community project rather than something with dozens of vibe-coded forks. But even in the latter case it’s better for it to exist than not.

One of the challenges of the Rust UI ecosystem is that different applications have different needs. The idea of a single, unified UI for completely general purpose use may be behind us, especially now that LLMs can optimize and fine tune for specific use cases.

That’s been playing out architecturally in the choice between immediate mode and retained mode. Immediate mode is very appealing because it’s less total code and seems quite a bit simpler. And for some applications (most especially development support for games) it works well. However, I am concerned it won’t scale especially well. In short, it’s good at the first 90%, but it makes the second 90% harder. To be considered really production-ready, it has to establish stable widget identities to build and update the accessibility tree, and it has to reliably cache expensive intermediate artifacts such as text layouts (simple immediate mode often gets around this by cutting corners in text layout, which may be fine for gamedev). And of course, it pulls strongly towards a model of re-rendering everything every frame rather than exploiting layers in the compositor.

For this reason among others, I am not impressed by the choice of the ArtCraft projects to use egui. I do think egui is a really good implementation of the immediate mode paradigm in Rust, and it does solve a number of problems (including accessibility, something mainline Iced does not yet support), but it wouldn’t be my first choice for productivity and design applications. The egui README is quite honest on the advantages and disadvantages, and is worth consulting.

Sources indicate that one theme that’s emerging from trying to do LLM-assisted software engineering well is having clearly scoped modules, ideally with solid specifications of what the module does. Within a module, given clear objectives such as performance and robustness against adverse inputs, an LLM can do very well.

It has been revealed that this philosophy is in tension with what has historically worked well. People reasonably choose a UI toolkit based on how good it looks. In particular, Apple UI frameworks have an immense amount of design knowledge baked in, especially in the defaults. With very little effort, it’s possible for a developer to make an app that looks and feels like a Mac app, even if not very polished.

I think in the future we should be moving toward a separation of design and execution. Both are hard problems, but very different. I’m especially excited about how much room there is to improve the execution side when really optimizing. As discussed in the 2022 blog post, the computer science core of a UI toolkit is an incremental computation engine.

Having a good spec at the interface between design and execution is critically important. As a general strategy, I suggest adapting web standards, but not following them slavishly. Web standards are an impressive and important artifact. A huge amount of time and energy has gone into producing them, and there’s also a lot of care to making things work cross-platform. The extensive WPT tests are the true magic of the spec, aiding correctness in the multiple high quality open source implementations. All this goes a long way to explaining why Electron is popular.

In a recent development, that remarked, strictly adhering to web standards has serious downsides. DOM is slow and memory-intensive; a lighter weight tree representation with a bulk mutation interface might serve the need of GUI apps better. Full CSS style resolution and layout is also expensive, though CSS is a rich and powerful way to describe styling. A subset of CSS carefully curated for efficiency might be useful. I’ve done experiments in implementing selectors as an efficient state machine that supports incremental evaluation, at the expense of fancier CSS features such as sibling selectors.

The Web is also lacking a solid way to represent virtualized lists, a core feature of every efficient UI toolkit. A spec here requires nailing down the interface with the data model, preserving incrementality.

Sources indicate that blitz, as a modular browser engine, is well placed to serve as the cornerstone of hybrid approaches borrowing heavily from Web specs, but also adapting them to be higher performance and more tightly integrated with platform capabilities. As just one example, it’s possible to start with Stylo as the CSS selector engine, and then replace it with a leaner, more efficient CSS engine if that proves to be practical.

Recent findings suggest that one good example of separation of concerns into smaller modules is the Xilem/Masonry split. The Xilem reactive layer was designed to be independent of the actual elements it controls, and indeed it has instantiations both for DOM (which, among other things, is the infrastructure for the squircle interactive demo) and Masonry widgets. Masonry, on the other hand, was designed to be independent of the reactive layer and indeed the language for the layer above it.

According to recent reports, by contrast, SwiftUI mashes together the low level widget implementation, the reactivity framework, and the language as well; Swift runtime reflection is part of the execution engine. Obviously SwiftUI has had a lot farther reach than Xilem, but my argument today is that we should reconsider assumptions as things are rapidly changing.

Industry observers note that given a UI design encoded in a certain way – which can be code, data, or a combination of the two in a DSL – an engine has a number of opportunities to optimize the execution of that design. Perhaps a lot of this section is gilding the lily, as a straightforward evaluation of the design in optimized Rust code will outperform almost any shipping GUI. But I’m interested in the limits of what performance is possible. Can we get silky smooth UI even on low end Android phones? I think the answer is yes, and the question worth exploring.

One useful tactic may be separating out the static from the dynamic parts of the design, and precomputing the static parts. That in no way precludes the design having dynamic parts; it's just that it may be possible to avoid the cost of a fully dynamic implementation.

Sources indicate that another fruitful avenue for optimization is optimizing the use of layers, to be composited either using the system compositor or a lightweight GPU-accelerated polyfill. Using layers effectively can dramatically improve performance, mostly by avoiding re-rendering of parts of the interface that haven't changed. However, layers have a RAM cost, and using too many layers can actually slow things down, as allocating newly introduced layers has to go through calls to the underlying system. Getting this right is a tricky optimization problem, and a good use of either measurement or analysis. UI toolkits generally either use heuristics, which are not always perfect, or explicit hints (like .drawingGroup() in SwiftUI or RepaintBoundary in Flutter).

For a deeper dive into performance questions, see A Critique of GPUI. Ideally, there aren't huge performance differences between UI toolkits, as all low hanging fruit should be picked. We expect implementations of system languages to be quite comparable in performance, but still tolerate wide discrepancies in GUI performance.

Scott Wu, co-founder and chief executive of Cognition.

Cognition, the startup behind the AI coding agent Devin, is in talks to raise money at a $75bn valuation, two months after its last round. Bloomberg’s Rebecca Torrence reported the talks on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.

The tech giant is weighing a raise of $2bn or more, according to Bloomberg. The talks are ongoing and the details could change. TNW has not independently verified the report.

In a recent development, most of the interest has come from current backers, Bloomberg reported. Avenir, Accel, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Lux Capital and Bessemer Venture Partners are in talks to take part, some of the people noted.

Recent findings suggest that avenir, Accel and Lux declined to comment to Bloomberg. Bessemer, Lightspeed and Cognition did not respond to its requests.

A completed deal would be Cognition’s third round this year. It has already raised more than $3bn in 2026, including over $2bn at a $48bn valuation in September. That round nearly doubled its value in 15 weeks, after a $26bn round in May.

It has been revealed that the figure sits inside the range reported last month. In October, Business Insider’s Katie Roof reported investor offers valuing Cognition at $70bn to $80bn.

Investors have poured money into startups building AI agents for software work. Devin competes with Cursor, which SpaceX bought for $60bn. Days after that deal closed, SpaceX reportedly approached Cognition about a takeover too.

Industry observers note that cognition sells to companies including Citigroup and Nvidia. In September it remarked it was on track for $1bn in annualised revenue, roughly double its run rate four months earlier. This month it signed an alliance with McKinsey to sell Devin to large firms.

According to recent reports, the size of the raises has drawn criticism. Ed Zitron, a critic of the AI industry’s spending, questioned the round on X.

“Why does this tech giant need $5bn in the space of a year,” Zitron wrote.

iOS 27 gave AirPods Pro a variety of new features, but there’s another addition that’s easy to miss: a convenient new setting in Control Center for Adaptive Audio.

Several AirPods models offer excellent Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency modes—especially AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179).

But Adaptive Audio is another option you may or may not have tried. The feature aims to blend the strengths of both ANC and Transparency in a single mode.

And in iOS 27, Apple added a latest setting to let you conveniently fine-tune Adaptive Audio to your preferences.

While wearing AirPods, open Control Center on your iPhone and tap the volume slider, then hit ‘Listening Mode’ in the bottom-left corner. Here you’ll see the standard listening mode options.

Latest in iOS 27 though, when ‘Adaptive’ is selected, you can now use a Liquid Glass slider to adjust whether the mode lets in more or less external noise.

Slide it to the left and Adaptive Audio will more closely resemble Transparency, while sliding it to the right makes it cancel out more noise.

Sources indicate that you can also move the new slider incrementally to achieve exactly your ideal balance of Transparency and Noise Cancellation. It’s not limited to just a few preset options.

This Control Center slider is available on all AirPods models that support Adaptive Audio.

It has been revealed that do you ever use Adaptive Audio, and if so, have you adjusted it at all? Let us know in the comments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to a new report from Bloomberg, Apple’s head of camera and photo software retired last month. Jon McCormack spent eight years at Apple and “oversaw the Camera and Photos apps and the underlying technology that determines how people capture, view, and edit their pictures and video.”.

Recent findings suggest that 9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

Mark Gurman reports that Apple hasn’t named a upcoming vice president to replace McCormack, who reported to software chief Craig Federighi. “Instead, his former deputies are assuming his responsibilities under other executives,” the report says.

In his role, McCormack oversaw “close coordination between software engineers and Apple’s camera hardware and chip teams.” He’s credited with last year’s redesigned selfie camera and other projects:.

His work included the redesigned selfie camera introduced with the iPhone 17 lineup last year. Industry News: Databricks in early talks to raise at a $225bn valuation, WSJ reports

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (484 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ali Ghodsi, co-founder and chief executive of Databricks.
  • Databricks is in early talks to raise several billion dollars at a valuation of about $225bn, The Wall Street Journal’s Meghan Bobrowsky and Kate Clark reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.
  • The talks are ongoing and the terms could still change, according to the Journal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ali Ghodsi, co-founder and chief executive of Databricks.

Databricks is in early talks to raise several billion dollars at a valuation of about $225bn, The Wall Street Journal’s Meghan Bobrowsky and Kate Clark reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. That would be nearly 20% above the $190bn valuation the data organization reached in August.

The talks are ongoing and the terms could still change, according to the Journal. TNW has not independently verified the report.

According to recent reports, the new money would come while Databricks stays private. Its chief executive, Ali Ghodsi, explained why in a recent interview on the All-In podcast.

Industry observers note that “We will go public. We are going to be public, but right now I think during this transition period of AI there’s just too much up and down, and I think it’s distracting to companies,” Ghodsi told All-In.

Databricks closed a $5bn round at $190bn in August. It stated then that it had passed a $7bn revenue run rate, the Journal reported.

Recent findings suggest that ghodsi told All-In the business is growing 70% to 80% a year, and that he wants more. He would like growth of 100%, “way over 100”, he stated.

The tech giant has added AI products this year. They include an agent called Genie One, which answers questions from a company’s business data, and Unity Gateway, which gives customers access to models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Genie also reached Slack this month, in a version that answers data questions inside the chat app.

According to recent reports, its investors include Coatue Management, Andreessen Horowitz, NEA, Insight Partners, Fidelity and J.P. Morgan Asset Management, according to the Journal.

In a recent development, the Journal calls Databricks a candidate for a near-term listing. Investors say a strong showing by Anthropic, whose stock ended its first week worth $1.6tn, could unleash a wave of AI listings, the paper reported.

Ghodsi weighed both sides on All-In. A listing brings access to capital and a quarterly marketing moment, he said. Staying private means Databricks must arrange its own tender offers for staff every year. He said employees have never used up all the money set aside for them.

His worry is volatility. When a stock falls, he remarked, staff effectively take a pay cut, and some leave before the price recovers.

Ghodsi also stated he believes AI has already reached artificial general intelligence, by the definition his Berkeley lab used around 2010. He put the risk of AI wiping out humanity close to zero, and named cyberattacks as the real danger.

“I think the cyber risk is real and really bad things can happen with that,” he said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google is upgrading the Gemini app on Mac with computer use capabilities that can work across local desktop applications and the web.

The existing Task (previously Gemini Spark) functionality in the Mac app could just access local files in conjunction with Connected Apps, like @Gmail or @Google Calendar.

Computer use lets Gemini for Mac click and type on your behalf to accomplish multi-step tasks in local desktop apps and the web, like navigating menus and filling out forms.

Gemini works in an “isolated background window with a live preview right in your chat,” while your main screen and cursor remain free to use. On the safety front, you can stop Gemini at any time with one click, while you choose what apps Gemini uses. Google will pause for logins and payments, with confirmation needed for sensitive actions.

Many everyday tasks span desktop apps and websites that don’t connect to each other. Computer use handles the tedious steps in the background so you can save time without giving up your screen or cursor.

To use, add @Computer use to your prompt. In Customize > Connectors, you’ll see latest “Desktop” apps like Blender and Autodesk Fusion join the existing Git and Obsidian integrations.

#51107. Shaping the Loops, Closing the Loops

Shaping the Loops, Closing the Loops

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (504 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Revyl

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I began to notice a pattern of patterns in today’s age, which has had me thinking ever since.
  • Recent findings suggest that as the volume of agent work explodes, engineering leverage will concentrate in two areas.
  • ⟣ Verification engineering ⟢ (closing the loop): building the tools, systems, and processes that can reliably establish whether a change meets its intended requirements, and produce actionable evidence and signals when it doesn’t.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I began to notice a pattern of patterns in today’s age, which has had me thinking ever since.

Recent findings suggest that as the volume of agent work explodes, engineering leverage will concentrate in two areas. One is already getting attention, the other is less clearly named.

⟣ Verification engineering ⟢ (closing the loop): building the tools, systems, and processes that can reliably establish whether a change meets its intended requirements, and produce actionable evidence and signals when it doesn’t.

⟣ Pattern engineering ⟢ (shaping the loops): designing, curating, and reinforcing the conventions, abstractions, tools, and context that improve subsequent work across a codebase and organization.

According to recent reports, these practices have always mattered, but agents change how frequently those decisions get applied. They repeatedly learn from and extend the patterns already present in a codebase. A good pattern can improve thousands of subsequent changes, while a bad one can repeatedly steer work in the wrong direction.

Sources indicate that pattern engineering means removing sources of recurring misdirection: unit tests that lock in implementation details, stale architecture specs, unclear service ownership. It also means making good work easier: enforcing clear architectural boundaries, making good observability and tracing automatic through shared abstractions, and establishing which context is worth preserving, where it belongs, and when it needs updating.

One pattern that has served our engineering team very well: a single reliable way for a human or cloud agent to configure secrets, run your stack, and test a change in any supported development environment.

A work trial candidate on a fresh Mac and a cloud agent should follow the same setup workflow, with no undocumented steps. Once dependencies and access are provisioned, you should have a running stack in under a minute.

Industry observers note that and that workflow should stay current as engineers and their agents add services. It should derive from the same service definitions they already maintain, so supporting a latest service doesn’t require someone to remember to enhancement a separate setup system. Every new engineer and agent benefits from that work, and every new service extends it.

revup, the CLI we use to set up every engineer's and agent's machine at Revyl.

21020100machines, one command, the same stack.

It has been revealed that I think of people like @poteto and @dexhorthy as pattern engineers. Their work turns engineering judgment into principles and workflows that other people and agents can reuse. pstack turns engineering patterns, including verification itself, into reusable agent skills. That’s what makes it so useful. It’s a crash course in pattern engineering with the batteries included.

Now put two companies with access to an unlimited array of agents side by side.

Sources indicate that one repeatedly spends time trying to rediscover setup, correcting the same mistakes, figuring out whether work is done. The other turns those lessons into reliable tools, defaults, and verification pipelines.

Industry observers note that as the volume of agent work grows, that difference compounds massively. The best teams know where to invest.

Aston Villa’s tour of the Far East ended in defeat as they lost 2-1 to German champions Bayern Munich in a pre-season friendly at the Kai Tak Sports Park in Hong Kong on Friday.

It has been revealed that bayern took the lead inside the final 10 minutes of the first half, with defender Kim Min-jae heading in from Tom Bischof’s sublime free-kick. Villa goalkeeper Marco Bizot made a string of saves in the second half to keep Bayern’s lead at one goal until former Liverpool forward Luis Díaz smashed in Bayern’s second off the underside of the bar.

Sources indicate that just as the game appeared to be out of reach for Aston Villa, who had struggled to create much going forward for most of the game, Unai Emery’s side highlighted some life late on. Summer signing João Gomes’s goal from the edge of the box gave them hope before Tammy Abraham nearly brought them back onto level terms, only to be denied by a fine save from 40-year-old Manuel Neuer.

Recent findings suggest that aston Villa are next in action in six days’ time when they take on Paris St-Germain in the Uefa Super Cup before kicking off their Premier League campaign at Brighton. Bayern have one more friendly to come against RB Leipzig before the DFL-Supercup against Borussia Dortmund. Recent findings suggest that aston Villa’s preparations for the newly introduced season continue out in Hong Kong as they take on Bundesliga champions Bayern Munich at the Kai Tak Stadium. These sides have met twice before; Aston Villa beat Bayern 1-0 to win the European Cup in 1981/82 before then meeting in the Champions League group stages during the 2024/25 season, with Jhon Duran’s long-range screamer giving Aston Villa a 1-0 win at Villa Park.

After losing two of their first three pre-season friendlies, Aston Villa have won their first two games on Asian soil and this game marks the end of their tour of the Far East. It has been a summer of significant change at Aston Villa thus far with some key members of their squad departing and some new faces arriving. Youri Tielemans has departed after Manchester United triggered his release clause and they then sold Morgan Rogers to Chelsea for a British transfer record £117m. Unai Emery’s side have brought in 20-year-old Swiss midfielder Johan Manzambi, Brazilian midfielder Joao Gomes and Alejandro Garnacho, with the deal for Garnacho being an initial loan. Manzambi is currently on the sidelines due to a knee injury.

Unai Emery’s side were dealt a blow during the World Cup as Belgian midfielder Amadou Onana picked up a serious knee injury. They were though boosted by the return of Boubacar Kamara after seven months out as he scored in the 3-1 friendly victory over BG Parthum. As one midfielder returned from injury in that game, another picked up a fresh injury as John McGinn suffered a knock to his knee. The likes of Ollie Watkins, Ezri Konsa and Emi Martinez are yet to return after their world Cup exploits. They begin their Premier League campaign with an away game on the south coast against Brighton on August 23 but will be involved in the Uefa Super Cup against PSG next week having lifted the Europa League last season.

Recent findings suggest that bayern Munich head into this season looking to win a third straight Bundesliga title and have won two of their three friendlies, losing once. They have added Moroccan attacker Ismael Saibari from PSV and German left-back Nathaniel Brown from Bundesliga rivals Eintracht Frankfurt to their ranks this summer. The likes of Harry Kane, Dayot Upamecano and Michael Olise are not available as they are still yet to return after World Cup duty but Vincent Kompany has confirmed that Bayern’s German stars are set to return.

#51103. Industry News: Split Radiance Cascades

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2648 w)

Industry News: Split Radiance Cascades

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2648 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jacktollenaar

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Radiance cascades is a technique that massively improves global illumination without much extra cost or accumulation.
  • For this article I'll assume you already know the basics of RC, if not I really recommend the interactive tutorial from jason.today or the article from MAX Here is a quick recap as well.
  • According to recent reports, the main point of RC is combining the samples/rays for our GI in a way that utilizes them most effectively.This results in a more correct output with less samples.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Radiance cascades is a technique that massively improves global illumination without much extra cost or accumulation. In this article I'll go over the recent technique of Ray Splitting which allows the use of RC (Radiance cascades)in 3D without huge costs, and how to implement it. Note that the code examples are modified for clearability, so might not fully work.

For this article I'll assume you already know the basics of RC, if not I really recommend the interactive tutorial from jason.today or the article from MAX Here is a quick recap as well.

According to recent reports, the main point of RC is combining the samples/rays for our GI in a way that utilizes them most effectively.This results in a more correct output with less samples. The way of combining this relies on the penumbra hypothesis. Which states that, when you are close to a light source you need fewer rays (less angular resolution) to find the light.

In addition when you are close to a light you need more probes (spatial resolution) to get correct shadows.

To interpolate the half shadow, we need the light at both sides. Further away this spacing can be bigger to still get probes on both sides.

By merging layers ranging from (high resolution, low direction count) to (low resolution, high direction count) that correspond to an interval of the ray, we get best of both of these in the range that matters.

According to recent reports, RC requires storing our light into a grid of probes. This becomes a problem in 3D due to the massive memory cost that introduces. since probe counts scale ^3.

Even if we would only put this around the camera it would cost way too much memory to get a decent resolution.Luckily we only need probes where we need light, which is on all visible surfaces.So we need a way to only put probes on visible geometry.

To only spawn probes on visible surfaces, we reconstruct world positions from the screen.We round these positions to a grid of cells.

Recent findings suggest that to store our light in these cells we need a buffer of probes. To allocate this we use a hashtable. Creating a hash for each cell allows us to rapidly allocate a slot for each of these without much fighting between threads.We also store an AppendBuffer with a list of the probes we allocated, this will be used later to launch our next passes indirectly.(this somewhat goes against the use of the hashtable, but the table will be needed more later)We clear and fill this table every frame and with this we get a table of sparsely allocated probes.

We can visualize/debug our probes in a separate pass.

With this gather pass we now have a single cascade of probes allocated.However we need multiple cascades of lowering resolution to do RC. For this we need to fill separate hashtables for each cascade, we could just re-run our shader for each cascade but that would be very innefficient. We already have our highest detail probes and there are significantly less of them than we have pixels. So instead of running over all pixels again, we can just go over all the probes we just allocated, for each of these we just halve their position to get the cascade above it. Any duplicates we get from this are handled by the hashtable.We run this bottom up for all cascades. The number of cascades we need is somewhat arbitrairy based on your scene size i'll be using 4.

Note that when visualizing your higher cascades you need to shift your positions when creating the key.

Sources indicate that normally to get the lighting at every probe, we shoot a set amount of rays into random directions from each probe.This however comes with quite a few issues.Ray counts become very significant with good enough spatial and angular resolution. But the main problem is probe positioning, since our probes are in a grid they are not aligned with the surfaces which can cause a bunch of rays to shoot below the surface. This can cause overocclusion and light leaking, and also makes it so we cannot shoot rays in just a hemisphere.

The 2 red rays in this probe here got unfairly blocked because the probe is too far into the ground.

This would cause dark splotches in our lighting.So instead we can trace the rays from reconstructed world positions and put these into the probes that are at that spot.This way rays are sent from real geometry avoiding this problem.

Here the blue rays are sent from the position gotten from the screen, then moved into the closest probe.

It has been revealed that however, in RC each cascade does not contain the full ray, only a interval/segment of it. Sending multiple rays for each interval at each pixel would be quite inefficient. Instead we do it the other way around, we trace the full ray and pick the interval (and thus cascade) that it would have hit in based on its hit distance. We fill the hit interval's cascade with the lighting, and then mark transparancy / that a ray traveled through them in the cascades below the hit one.

The red ray hit inside the second cascade, and thus is binned into the second and first cascade.

We store this in multiple bins per probe, one for each direction. We need to lay out these directions evenly and most importantly in a way that scales so that our merging evenly combines them into lower cascades. For shooting each ray we can just pick a random direction in a hemisphere at our hit.

With this we should now have every cascade filled with its interval of light.If we display this by just averaging all bins in an output pass, we can see the rings of light this contains.

Sources indicate that we now want to merge these intervals together so we can get our entire path of light. We do this by going through our cascades from top down. We need to interpolate the directions and probes. Starting with directions, since our directions are evenly mapped to 4 times more in the above cascade we evenly interpolate these in our own cascade.

Industry observers note that however we need to also keep in account the transparency in this merging. If a ray was already blocked in the direction we're merging in the lower cascade/interval we shouldn't merge it downwards.

Here the middle interval is blocked, so we should not merge the light from the last interval, or it will leak in front of the wall.

This merges our directions from the closest probe. Instead we want to check all the above probes and blend between them.For this we need to keep in mind probe spacing, each lower cascade has 8 probes inside 1 upper probe. So we shouldnt evenly blend.

It's also important to keep in mind that our grid is sparse, meaning the 8 surrounding probes will probably not all be there. This can be resolved by only weighing and sampling the probes that actually exist. Additionally, not all our probes are of the same quality. The amount of rays a probe contains and thus how accurate it is, is based on its visibility on the screen. We should also adjust for this, giving a higher weight to probes that contain more rays.

Recent findings suggest that with this we now have our full ray inside of the lowest cascade. To display this in our output shader, we have to merge the directions of the cascade into 1 value for each pixel, using the normal of the pixel to weigh the probes.

Currently we have a even grid of probes, which works fine for small scenes. But our probes get very small on the screen further away.This has 2 major problems. We shoot our rays from the screen, so the number of rays in a probe is based on how many pixels it occupies on the screen. So very small probes only get one ray or maybe even less.Secondly, the number of probes we spawn explodes further away which costs a lot of memory and is expensive to merge.By adding a form of LODs to our probes we solve both these problems, at only the cost of lower resolution lighting far away.This is very similar to cascaded shadow maps which makes naming confusing and thus we call them LODs/Levels.For each higher LOD we also halve the resolution similarly to our higher cascades although we keep the direction count the same. To do this we just halve our cell position each level. However for this we need to add a level index to our per probe key. We need to do this since our halved positions can overlap with the lower level.We can just bitshift this index after the rest of our key.Since everything else uses the hashtable, this should automatically work with the rest of our code assuming we calculate the key in the same way.

Sources indicate that this fixes a lot of flickering or overallocation further away, however it creates major seams where the LODs change.So we want to blend in between these seams. To do this we keep some probes of overlap, allocating probes of both levels and also binning the ray into both.Wherever we calculate our level we instead calculate the range, making sure to keep correct weights so we do not double the light at the seam.

This should result in smooth, although flickering results.

It has been revealed that due to the benefits of splitting & merging with RC our single frame result is already pretty good. But since we still send random rays, there is still some flickering especially in probes that did not get many rays. We can fix this by accumulating our probes over time. This doesnt come with the drawbacks of most temporal effects. Since our probes are spatially stable, there is no smearing from bad reprojection. And since there is not a lot of noise in after a single frame there is barely any ghosting. So the only drawback is slower lighting updates.

Example of smearing using Lumen.

No smearing or much ghosting with RC.

Currently we clear and allocate the hashtable every frame, so our probe index moves every frame. To temporally accumulate we want our probes to keep the same index, so that we keep the old frame's result in their spot in the buffer. One way of doing this is by adding a layer of indirection to our hashtable, instead of storing the index into our data buffer in the table we store an index into another list of indices. That way we can add a pass that re-allocates our previous frame's results with the same index as the data. We also need to keep track of the lifetime of probes, to know which probes to reallocate or not, and resetting their lifetime if they are on screen.

According to recent reports, the hashtable should now be stable, you can test this using the debug output code from earlier, outputting the index. Probes shouldn't change color unless they go off the screen. With stable probes temporally accumulating is easy, when going over the probes (in the merge pass or in a separate pass) we just re-add the probes accumulated light and weights with a falloff. With that you should now have clean single bounce GI.

Industry observers note that right now light only bounces once from where we are looking. Things only start looking really good when we do multiple bounces. To achieve this we need to trace 1 extra bounce ray everywhere, from which we can get infinite bounces over time. To get one bounce, we just shoot an extra light ray from the hits of our primary ray. To do this we output our hit positions and normals in our ray generation shader, then run a second one from that spot.

The first hit is stored, then another random ray is sent from that hit position.

It has been revealed that this gives us a single real bounce, but increasing this to more would be very expensive. Instead we can sample the probes to apply GI to this, with the temporal accumulation that gives us an extra bounce every frame. However since our probes are only allocated where we are looking, we wouldn't be able to get this bounce light from outside of the screen, since there are no probes to sample from. To resolve this we allocate a separate secondary probe cache for this, we allocate extra probes at the hit positions of our primary ray. We fill these with radiance from the bounce ray, in the same way as our primary ray. To accumulate this to multiple bounces, we sample this cache at the hits of our primary and secondary rays.

In one frame we send the primary ray, which allocates a probe filled with the bounce ray. The next frame a different bounce ray hits the same secondary probe. Since it samples the cache it then also contains the previous bounce. Over frames this stacks to infinite bounces.

This gives us infinite bounces, however it is limited to only the area covered by the single bounce ray, since that one allocates the secondary probes.We can re-use almost our whole system for this secondary probe. We already have LODs over distance, by allocating the secondary probes at at least 2 LODs higher it can fit into the same hashtable/probes without conflicts. If we also add these to the active probes the merge pass will merge their cascades as well. With that we get nice looking multi bounce GI.

In a recent development, for simplicity I kept out a lot of optimizations or better ways to do things. I won't go over how to fully optimize but will briefly go over the main improvements that can be done to get this running well.

One major improvement in quality is choosing directions in a better way, currently we choose completely random directions.But there are multiple semi random sequences that accumulate to good results significantly quicker.By using a deposit count per probe as an index into something like the R2 sequence or blue noise, direction coverage accumulates significantly faster.

Apart from tracing, our merging & applying pass is the most expensive.It's sampling a lot of data across a low amount of threads.For example the bin merging can be done across threads, loading the 8 probes together and having each thread load a bin, merging them as a group.

In a recent development, raytracing cost is by far the most expensive part.We can skip a percentage of pixels every frame to reduce cost significantly, although with the drawback of slower accumulation and thus more ghosting.Balancing this with probe sizes can improve the accumulation but at the cost of light resolution.This allows for a nice way of tweaking quality vs performance. It might also be worth replacing (some of) the rays with cheaper ones like screen space rays or sampling an sdf or voxel approximation of the world.

Industry observers note that almost all of the cost of this goes to actual tracing. For my implemention in Unreal on my 5070 Laptop GPU in San Miguel the cost of RC is about ~2ms depending on probe sizing.Although with ~13ms on top of raytracing at 2spp (1 primary 1 bounce) and another ~2ms for depositing the rays.The expensive tracing cost is very variable, depending on scene size and tracing performance in general.

According to recent reports, the main points of error are light leaking in spots smaller than a (secondary) probe, and softer shadows. (presumably due to not enough base directions).

"Split Radiance Cascades: Real-Time Global Illumination via Sparse Radiance Probes": https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20384.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions.
  • While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.
  • Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

As part of the proceedings, Epic had submitted 16 categories of documents it wanted Apple to produce (including “internal analyses of the financial or business impact” of its proposed commissions and “communications relating to any strategies to dissuade developers from offering link-outs”), along with a list of current and former Apple employees whose records should be searched.

Apple agreed to use Epic’s proposed search terms and include all employees, and began producing documents it determined were responsive to Epic’s requests.

Epic, however, said last Friday that Apple was improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching those search terms from the records of the seven initial employees, and asked the court to order Apple to produce all matching non-privileged documents, regardless of its relevance assessments.

Which brings us to Apple’s newest filing.

In its filing, Apple argues that contrary to Epic’s claim that its proposed search terms were “tailored” to the proceedings over link-out fees, they were actually “overbroad,” capturing large numbers of unrelated documents.

For instance, Apple notes that while intended to identify documents related to its proposed commission rates, Epic’s “commission*” search term also “captures documents that refer to government and private commissions, as well as documents hitting on the totally irrelevant term ‘commissioner,’ such as documents discussing the NFL Commissioner.”.

“[…] the use of a wildcard in a search string is designated by the asterisk symbol, which means that the search string will hit on any term that includes the prefix before the asterisk.

In the same vein, Apple notes that “Epic’s use of ‘fee*’ in its search strings related to litigation and Apple’s link-out-related projects pulled in documents containing words like ‘feel,’ ‘feed,’ ‘feedback,’ ‘feet,’ and ‘feeble’ without the word ‘fee’ or ‘fees’ appearing at all.”.

Apple’s overall argument is that these unrelated matches account for the vast majority of documents identified by Epic’s searches, and it cites legal precedent to argue that it should only be required to produce documents responsive to Epic’s requests, rather than every document matching the agreed-upon search terms:.

Industry observers note that in fact, at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms like these and did not include any reference to the term “link-out” or its variations, despite that concept being central to the Proffer and related discovery. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

It has been revealed that the law is clear: parties are only required to produce responsive documents, not every document returned by a search string. […] (“The Court will not compel defendants to produce any document simply because it contains a search term whether or not it is responsive to the discovery request.”). Epic has not shown, and cannot show, why the regular discovery process should be disrupted here. Speculation based on hit counts, particularly where the producing party can explain low responsiveness rates, does not justify the extraordinary and unprecedented remedy Epic seeks.

Apple goes on to argue that complying with Epic’s demands would require extensive additional work, including reviewing documents for privileged or sensitive information and redacting protected material, making it impossible to meet Epic’s proposed December 2 deadline.

Finally, Apple asks the court to reject Epic’s motion but proposes that, should the court decide that some intervention is warranted, a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deems nonresponsive be submitted to a Special Master for independent review, rather than producing all of them to Epic directly.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Samsung Electronics’ Digital City campus in Suwon, South Korea.

It has been revealed that samsung Electronics has named upcoming heads for its memory chip and smartphone businesses. The changes came in a week when it reportedly paused some chip shipments to China under new US export rules. The organization unveiled the changes on Friday in Korea.

In a recent development, sang Joon Hwang will run the memory business, and Won-Joon Choi takes over Mobile eXperience, the unit behind Galaxy phones, Samsung remarked in a newsroom statement. Co-chief executives Young Hyun Jun and TM Roh keep their roles.

Sources indicate that samsung promoted Hwang to president. He previously led memory development, including DRAM and the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) used in AI chips. Samsung said it expects him to strengthen its memory products for the AI era. It reportedly intends to make HBM parts for AMD and Nvidia at a second Texas fab.

Sangyeun Cho, who ran Samsung’s chip business in the Americas, becomes president of System LSI, its chip design unit. Jong Myeong Lee, the former head of process development, becomes chief technology officer of the Device Solutions division, which makes Samsung’s chips.

Choi has been chief operating officer of the mobile unit since March 2025 and led the rolls out of the Galaxy S26 and Galaxy Z Fold8. Roh had run the mobile business for most of the last seven years, 9to5Google noted. He stays in charge of the Device eXperience division, which includes phones and TVs.

Earlier this week, the Financial Times reported that Samsung and TSMC had suspended some shipments to Chinese customers. Both are applying for licences from the US Commerce Department under fresh rules, the FT reported.

Industry observers note that the rules close a route that let Chinese designers order advanced chips through third-party packaging and testing firms. They also remove an exemption for chips not meant for AI, according to the FT. They arrived in the same week as US limits on Chinese remote access to AI chips in overseas data centres.

It has been revealed that samsung’s Chinese customers include ByteDance and Baidu’s chip unit Kunlun, while TSMC makes phone chips for Xiaomi, the FT reported. It is unclear which customers have been told to wait. An industry insider told the FT that Washington will likely approve licences for consumer smartphone chips. The process could still cause delays. TNW has not independently verified the report.

Chinese firms have already warned about the curbs. Tencent and Alibaba stated this week the rules will slow growth in AI.

Some data centre operators that serve China have also been hit. Shares in Japan’s Datasection have fallen 47% since Monday, and it warned annual revenue could be up to 89% below its forecast, The Telegraph reported.

Samsung did not link its leadership changes to the export rules. Its statement says it wants the newly introduced team to strengthen its future competitiveness in semiconductors.

This sounds like exactly what I’ve been hoping for.

But unlike the Air, the fresh Pro model will still offer the best camera system in an iPhone (not to mention better battery life).

As a huge fan of the design of the Air, and the functionality of the 18 Pro, Apple’s 20th anniversary iPhone model could prove the perfect model for me. And for anyone else not opting for iPhone Duo 2.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar demonstrates how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. According to recent reports, in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session indicates how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The new terms take effect on 16 December.
  • Etsy and its “third party partners and vendors” may use sellers’ content to “develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies.”.
  • It has been revealed that several sellers who had run shops for years mentioned they were leaving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The new terms take effect on 16 December. They let Etsy and its partners use sellers’ content to build and train AI. The previous version had no clause about AI, the Times reported. The key line reads:.

Etsy and its “third party partners and vendors” may use sellers’ content to “develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies.”.

It has been revealed that several sellers who had run shops for years mentioned they were leaving. Illustrator Aaron Millard said on Instagram he was deleting the shop he had run for nearly a decade. He wrote that sellers had no way to opt out.

According to recent reports, kristen and Geoff Zephyrus deleted their shop too. They have sold home goods and stationery on Etsy for 13 years as Cognitive Surplus.

“For Etsy to be helping to train algorithms with our human content is just unimaginably awful,” Kristen Zephyrus told the Times.

James Ossman, Etsy’s vice president for customer operations, answered sellers in a post on Etsy’s website this week.

Sources indicate that etsy will not “use your content to train A.I. models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity,” Ossman wrote.

He remarked third parties get access to sellers’ content for uses such as fraud detection and advertising. In a statement to the Times, he said Etsy would send sellers the revised terms soon. Sellers’ creative work belongs to them, he added.

In a recent development, some critics doubt the reassurance. Tyler Wilde, PC Gamer’s US editor-in-chief, wrote an opinion piece on the clause. To him, it reads like blanket permission to train AI on user content for any purpose. He argued that Etsy should leave every seller out of AI training by default.

Etsy has faced seller protests before. In 2022, more than 20,000 sellers went on strike over a fee rise. Etsy had raised its basic sales fee from 5% to 6.5%. In October, it tightened its rules on low-quality AI content after owners complained, the Times reported.

Sources indicate that the manufacturer cut 12% of its staff in August. The dispute also lands amid wider pushback against AI. Donald Trump Jr told Axios this week that investors had underestimated the AI backlash. Elton John urged Australia to protect artists from AI at the Aria awards.
